title: Perception: why your brain picks one reading of the world, and what it leaves out

summary.text: A cube drawn with plain lines suddenly flips: the corner that pointed towards you now points away. Nothing on the paper changed, and you cannot see both cubes at once. Your child counts the flips in one minute. Then they change one thing on a tray while a card hides it for a second, and find that a watcher can take many seconds to notice. They find out how many F's people miss in a sentence, whether a face is easier to read the right way up, and how a tiny paper beetle can vanish into a pattern. The unit follows one idea. The brain has to pick one way of making sense of what it sees, called a reading. It picks using what you expect and what you pay attention to, and it leaves out the rest.
summary.art: A girl at a table looking at a cube drawn in lines on paper, with two faint thought bubbles beside her head showing the cube pointing one way and then the other.

intro.hook: Read this and count the letter F. FINISHED FILES ARE THE RESULT OF YEARS OF SCIENTIFIC STUDY COMBINED WITH THE EXPERIENCE OF YEARS. Many people find three. There are six. Where did the others go?
intro.text: Your eyes took in every letter. But your brain was busy reading for meaning, and it slid over the little word 'of' as if it were not there. The word 'of' appears three times, so three F's went uncounted. You did not choose to miss them. In this unit you meet other cases where the brain makes one reading and drops the rest. A cube drawing flips by itself. A big change in a tray goes unseen. You see faces in plug sockets and clouds. A paper beetle vanishes against a cloth. You test each one on yourself and on your family. Then you ask what it means that each of us gets only one reading of the world.
intro.art: A sentence in big capital letters on a card, with six of the letter F circled in red, and a girl looking surprised beside it.

outcomes: I can explain, using a cube drawing, that a picture can have two readings and that my brain shows me only one at a time.
I can explain what attention does, and why I can look straight at a big change and not see it.
I can explain how what I expect changes what I read and what I find, using the letter F test and a hidden object.
I can explain how the brain groups bits into wholes, and how it can show me shapes that are not drawn.
I can explain why a face is harder to read upside down, and why I see faces in clouds, walls and fronts of scooters.
I can explain that two people can see the same thing differently, and that animals live in different sensory worlds from mine.
I can explain how camouflage works by fooling the way the brain groups things and what it expects.
I can plan a fair test with several people, collect the results, and say what they show without claiming too much.

terms.meaning: The way the brain turns the signals from your senses into what you see, hear, feel, taste and smell. It is made by the brain, not just recorded.
terms.example: You perceive a friend's face at once, though the signals from your eyes are only patterns of light.
terms.art: A girl looking at a friend, with thin lines running from her eyes to a brain that is drawing a face.

terms.meaning: One way of making sense of something that could be understood in more than one way. A drawing, a word or a sound can have more than one reading.
terms.example: The same drawing can be read as a vase or as two faces.
terms.art: A single line drawing in the middle, with an arrow to a vase on one side and an arrow to two faces on the other.

terms.meaning: Able to mean two or more things equally well. An ambiguous drawing or sentence has more than one reading.
terms.example: 'I saw her duck' is ambiguous. It could mean a bird or a quick bend.
terms.art: A sentence on a board with two small drawings beneath it, a duck and a person ducking.

terms.meaning: A drawing of a cube made only with lines, so that it can be read as pointing in two ways. It flips by itself as you look. It is named after the Swiss scientist Louis Albert Necker.
terms.example: Look at the cube for half a minute, and it will flip from one reading to the other.
terms.art: A cube drawn with all twelve edges visible, with two arrows showing which corner can seem to point towards you.

terms.meaning: The brain's way of choosing a few things to deal with in detail. What you do not attend to gets very little detail.
terms.example: In a noisy market, you hear your own name because you attend to it.
terms.art: A girl in a crowded market with a bright spotlight on her friend's face and the rest of the crowd faded.

terms.meaning: Missing something clear and large because your attention is on something else. It happens to people with good eyesight too.
terms.example: People counting passes of a ball in a video often miss a person in a gorilla suit who walks through.
terms.art: A video screen with players passing a ball and a small gorilla in the corner, and a viewer staring at the ball.

terms.meaning: Not noticing a big change in a scene because something hid the moment of change, such as a blink or a flash.
terms.example: A cloth passes in front of your face. While it hides your view, the person in front of you swaps places with someone else, and you do not notice.
terms.art: Two photos of the same street scene that differ in one big thing, with a blank grey picture between them.

terms.meaning: What the brain thinks is likely before it looks. Expectation speeds up seeing, and also makes you miss things that do not fit.
terms.example: You read 'Paris in the the spring' and often miss the doubled word.
terms.art: A sign reading Paris in the the spring with a pair of eyes skipping over the second word.

terms.meaning: A picture in the mind of what you are looking for. It helps you find that thing quickly, and hides other things.
terms.example: A bird that has been eating green caterpillars goes on looking for green ones, and passes brown ones.
terms.art: A bird on a branch with a thought bubble of a green caterpillar, and a brown caterpillar beside her unnoticed.

terms.meaning: The brain's habit of joining nearby, similar or connected bits into one thing. The German scientist Max Wertheimer described it in the 1920s. It is also called a Gestalt rule.
terms.example: Dots in a tight cluster look like one shape, though each dot is separate.
terms.art: A page of dots in rows with some dots drawn closer together, forming clear groups.

terms.meaning: The brain's choice of what is the thing (the figure) and what is the background behind it (the ground). Which is which can swap.
terms.example: In the vase drawing, the vase is the figure, until the faces become the figure.
terms.art: A black and white vase drawing with the vase shaded in one colour and the faces shaded in another.

terms.meaning: An edge that you see although nothing is drawn there. The brain makes the edge to complete a shape.
terms.example: In the ghost triangle, you see white edges that are not on the paper.
terms.art: Three black circles with wedges cut out and three corners of lines, with a white triangle seen between them.

terms.meaning: Seeing a face, or another familiar shape, in something that is not one, such as a cloud, a wall stain or a pair of sockets and a switch.
terms.example: A plug socket often looks like a surprised face.
terms.art: A wall with a plug socket and a switch that look like a surprised face.

terms.meaning: The fact that faces are harder to recognise upside down than other objects are. It shows that the brain has a special way of reading upright faces.
terms.example: You know your friend's photo at once, but not as quickly when it is upside down.
terms.art: A photo of a smiling girl upright, and the same photo turned upside down beside it.

terms.meaning: Colours or patterns that make a living being hard to find. It works by matching the background, or by breaking up the outline.
terms.example: A tiger's stripes break up her outline in tall grass.
terms.art: A tiger lying in tall dry grass, her stripes almost matching the grass stems.

terms.meaning: The brain's habit of seeing the colour of a thing as steady, though the colour of the light changes. It allows a banana to look yellow indoors and outdoors.
terms.example: A white shirt looks white both in sunshine and under a yellow bulb.
terms.art: A white shirt in two pictures, one in blue-white daylight and one in yellow lamp light, both labelled white.

terms.meaning: The part of the world that an animal can sense and act on. Different animals have different umwelten. The word is German for surroundings, and the idea comes from the biologist Jakob von Uexküll.
terms.example: A tick waits on a leaf for the smell of sweat and the warmth of a body. That is most of her world.
terms.art: A tick on a grass blade with faint lines for the smell and the warmth of an animal, and nothing else drawn in their world.

terms.meaning: Two directions of seeing. Bottom-up starts with the signals from the eyes. Top-down starts with what the brain already knows and expects. Seeing uses both together.
terms.example: You find a friend in a crowd faster because you expect to see them wearing a blue shirt.
terms.art: Two arrows on a brain, one going up from the eyes and one coming down from the memory, meeting in the middle.

explanations.concept: Perception is a best guess, and the brain shows you only one
explanations.definition: Perception is the brain's reading of the signals from the senses. The signals alone usually fit more than one reading, so the brain chooses the most likely one and shows you only that.
explanations.description: Light that enters the eye is a pattern of brightness and colour. The same pattern could come from many different scenes. A small thing close by and a big thing far away can look the same size to the eye. A flat drawing of a cube can be read as a cube pointing two ways. The brain has to pick, because a body must act on one reading at a time. You cannot reach for a cube that is both near and far. So the brain uses clues, and what it expects, to pick the likeliest reading, and it shows you that. You never see 'maybe'. About a thousand years ago, the scientist Ibn al-Haytham wrote that seeing is not only the light that enters the eye. He said that recognising what we see also needs memory and judgment, though we do not notice ourselves doing it. In the 1860s, Hermann von Helmholtz called this unconscious inference, which means that the brain draws conclusions without our noticing.
examples: A distant bus looks tiny but you read it as a normal bus far away, not as a toy bus close by.
A face drawn with a few lines still reads as a face.
A dark shape on a night road reads as a rock, a dog or a bag, depending on what you expect.
explanations.art: A pair of eyes sending the same small shape to a brain, which has two thought bubbles, a small near ball and a big far ball, with a tick on one.
explanations.context: This card explains why a picture can have two readings, and why the brain shows only one.

explanations.concept: Pictures with two readings: the cube, the vase and the duck-rabbit
explanations.definition: An ambiguous picture is a drawing that fits two readings about equally well. You see one reading at a time, and your brain flips between them without your choosing.
explanations.description: In 1832, the Swiss crystal expert Louis Albert Necker described a drawing of a crystal that seemed to turn inside out as he watched. We now call it the Necker cube. In 1915, the Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin published the vase and faces drawing. In it, the vase and the faces share the same edge, and you see either a vase or two faces. In 1899, the American psychologist Joseph Jastrow made famous a drawing that looks like a duck facing left or a rabbit facing right. In every case the lines never change. The flip happens in the brain. Most people can slow the flips by trying to hold one reading, but few can stop them. The flips seem to come when one reading has been seen for a while and the other reading takes over. You cannot see both readings at the same moment. One reading is always the figure, the thing in front. The other becomes the background behind it. Scientists have found brain activity that changes at each flip, but they do not yet fully know why the brain flips.
examples: A cube drawn with all twelve edges visible flips in and out.
The vase and faces drawing flips between a vase and two faces looking at each other.
The duck-rabbit flips between a duck looking left and a rabbit looking right.
explanations.art: Three ambiguous drawings in a row, the cube, the vase and faces, and the duck-rabbit, each with two small arrows showing the two readings.
explanations.context: This card explains the Count the Flips test and the other drawings that can be read in two ways.

explanations.concept: Attention: you see in detail only what you attend to
explanations.definition: The eye takes in a wide view, but the brain deals with only a few things in detail. Attention is how it chooses. Things that are not attended to can go unseen, even when they are large and in front of you.
explanations.description: In 1975, Ulric Neisser and Robert Becklen played two videos on top of each other, a hand-slapping game and a ball game. People who followed one game often missed odd things in the other. In 1999, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked people to count the passes made by players in white shirts in a video. About half of the viewers did not see a person in a gorilla suit who walked right through the middle and beat her chest. In 1998, Simons and Daniel Levin had a person stop strangers to ask for directions. While the stranger was giving directions, workers carrying a door passed between them, and the person asking was swapped for a different person. About half of the strangers did not notice that they were talking to someone new. In 1997, Ronald Rensink and others showed that if a blank flash covers the moment of a big change in a photograph, people take many flashes to find it. Without the flash, the change pops out at once, because the brain notices movement. These results are not signs of poor eyesight or carelessness. They show that detailed seeing needs attention.
examples: You do not notice your own nose until you are told to think about it.
A driver on the phone can look at a red light and still not see it.
You miss your mother's new haircut for a whole day.
explanations.art: A video screen showing players in white shirts passing a ball, a gorilla in the middle of the screen, and a viewer with a pencil counting and not looking at the gorilla.
explanations.context: This card explains the Blink Tray test and why you can miss big changes right in front of you.

explanations.concept: Expectation and search images: you find what you look for
explanations.definition: The brain uses what it expects to read and to search quickly. This helps when the world is as expected, and causes misses when something does not fit.
explanations.description: When you read, your eyes jump from word to word. They often skip short, common words, because the brain can guess them. That is why many people miss the extra 'the' in 'Paris in the the spring', and the letters F in the word 'of'. A related idea is the search image. In 1960, the Dutch scientist Luuk Tinbergen noticed that small birds in pine woods ate a kind of insect mostly when that insect was common, and he suggested that a bird learns a picture of what to look for. In 1971, Marian Dawkins reported tests on young chicks. Chicks that had found one type of grain over and over were slower to find a second type, even when the second was easy to see. Searching for one kind of thing seems to make the brain pay less attention to others. The same happens to people looking for a lost key, for a friend in a crowd, or for a leaf insect on a bush. If you look for a bug sitting on a leaf, you may pass a bug who looks like a leaf.
examples: You find your own slippers in a pile of chappals quickly, because you know what they look like.
A mother looking for her child's blue school uniform in a crowd does not notice the people in red shirts.
A birdwatcher who looks for a big bird misses the small one.
explanations.art: A bush full of green leaves with one leaf insect in the middle, circled faintly, and a man's eyes looking at a bug-shaped thought bubble.
explanations.context: This card explains the F test and why you can overlook what you are not looking for.

explanations.concept: Grouping and ghost shapes: the brain joins bits into wholes
explanations.definition: The brain joins nearby, similar and connected bits into whole things. It can even draw edges that are not there, to complete a shape. These edges are called illusory contours.
explanations.description: In the 1920s, Max Wertheimer and other German scientists described how we group what we see. We join things that are close together, things that look alike, things that move together, and things that make a closed shape. In 1955, the Italian scientist Gaetano Kanizsa drew three black circles, each with a wedge cut out, set so that the wedges point to the middle. Most people see a white triangle lying on top, with clear edges. The edges are not drawn. In 1984, Rüdiger von der Heydt and his team found nerve cells in the visual part of a monkey's brain that responded to these edges that do not exist, as if they were real lines. Grouping is useful. In the real world, an animal in leaves is often seen only in pieces. The brain joins the pieces into a whole animal. It does not always have enough information to be right.
examples: Dots arranged in rows look like rows, though each is separate.
The stars of a constellation look like one shape, such as a hunter, though the stars are far apart.
A half-hidden cat behind a fence still looks like one cat.
explanations.art: Three black circles with wedges removed, arranged so that a white triangle seems to float in front, with its faint edges shown as dotted lines.
explanations.context: This card explains the Ghost Triangle activity and how the brain completes shapes.

explanations.concept: Faces: a special skill, and faces everywhere
explanations.definition: Humans are very good at recognising upright faces. The skill depends on the whole face being seen the right way up, and it fails when the face is turned upside down. The brain also finds faces in things that are not faces.
explanations.description: In 1969, Robert Yin showed that faces are harder to recognise upside down than other objects are. In 1980, the British scientist Peter Thompson turned the eyes and mouth of a photo of a famous face upside down inside the face. Held upright, the face looked horrible. Turned upside down, it looked almost normal. This is called the Thatcher effect, after the photo he used. It shows that the brain reads an upright face as a whole, and that the strangeness of the changed parts becomes clear only in the upright face. In 1997, Nancy Kanwisher and her team found a part on the underside of the brain that responds strongly to faces. This skill starts early. Tests reported in the 1970s and 1990s found that newborn babies look longer at face-like patterns than at the same patterns jumbled. The skill is so sensitive that it responds even to two dots and a line. That is why we see faces in sockets, scooters, clouds and a burnt chapati.
examples: A plug socket with two holes and a switch looks like a surprised face.
The front of a scooter looks like a face with two eyes and a nose.
A photo of someone you know is harder to recognise upside down.
explanations.art: A face photo upright with a changed mouth that looks horrible, and the same photo turned upside down looking almost normal.
explanations.context: This card explains the Upside-Down Faces test and why you see faces in objects.

explanations.concept: Camouflage works by fooling how the brain reads
explanations.definition: Camouflage is a pattern or shape that helps an animal avoid being found. It works either by matching the background, or by breaking up the animal's outline so that the brain does not read it as one animal.
explanations.description: In 1940, the British zoologist Hugh Cott described many kinds of camouflage in animals. In background matching, an animal is coloured like the place where they live, like a moth on tree bark. In disruptive colouring, dark and light patches run across the body edge and cut it into pieces that the brain joins to the background instead. A tiger's stripes in tall dry grass do this. In 2005, a team led by Innes Cuthill put paper moths on tree trunks. Birds found the moths whose patterns cut across the edge less often than the moths whose patterns did not. Some animals go further. The leaf butterfly Kallima, found in India, folds her wings to look like a dead leaf with veins and spots. Leaf insects look like green leaves, with veins and sometimes marks like bites. In all these cases the hunter has a search image, a picture in mind of what to look for. The camouflage makes the animal look like something else that the hunter expects to see there, such as a leaf. It is a trick played on the brain, and not on the eyes.
examples: A nightjar sitting on the ground looks like a dead leaf or a stone, and she is hard to see.
A stick insect holds still and looks like a twig.
A leaf butterfly with wings folded looks like a dry leaf.
explanations.art: A tiger half hidden in tall grass, a leaf butterfly folded like a dead leaf, and a stick insect on a twig, each with a faint outline drawn.
explanations.context: This card explains the Hide the Beetle challenge and how camouflage fools the brain.

explanations.concept: Every animal lives in a world of their own: the umwelt
explanations.definition: Each kind of animal senses only part of the world, and acts in that part. That part is called the umwelt. Different animals have different umwelten.
explanations.description: In the 1930s, the Estonian-German biologist Jakob von Uexküll described the umwelt with the example of a tick. A tick can wait on a leaf for a very long time, and drops onto an animal when she smells a chemical in sweat and feels warmth. Her world is very small. Honeybees see ultraviolet light, which we cannot see. Many flowers have patterns in ultraviolet that guide bees to the nectar, and a flower that looks plain to us can look striped to a bee. Dogs have two kinds of colour sensor, and we have three, so a dog sees fewer colours than we do. But a dog has a far larger share of the brain for smell, and a world of smells that we can hardly imagine. Bats find insects in the dark by sound echoes. Pit vipers sense heat. None of these animals senses the whole world. Neither do we. Each of us gets one reading, from one body.
examples: A bee sees ultraviolet stripes on a flower that looks plain to us.
A dog follows a smell trail across a road that we cannot smell at all.
A bat's world is made of echoes.
explanations.art: A flower shown twice, once plain yellow as a child sees it, and once with a dark ultraviolet target pattern as a bee sees the flower.
explanations.context: This card explains why other animals do not sense the same world as we do, and what that tells us.

explanations.concept: The dress: the same photo, different colours
explanations.description: In February 2015, a photo of a dress spread across the world. Some people saw it as blue and black. Others saw it as white and gold. The photo itself had one set of colours, so the different answers had to come from the people. Scientists think that the brain tries to remove the colour of the light to find the true colour of the cloth, and that it is not sure what light the dress is in. If the brain assumes the dress is in bluish shade, it removes blue and sees white and gold. If it assumes the dress is in yellowish lamp light, it removes yellow and sees blue and black. Scientists disagree about why people assume different light. One study found that people who are awake early and spend more time in daylight saw it differently from people who stay up late. Others have not found the same, so the idea is not settled.
examples: A white cloth looks white in the shade, though the shade is bluish.
A friend says a shirt is green, and you say it is blue.
A photo of a shoe looks different in sunlight and under a tube light.

perspectives.explanation: The brain takes away the colour of the light it expects. People who expect different light see different colours in the same photo.
A person's own life, such as time spent in daylight or in lamp light, may set what light they expect. Some tests found support for this, and others did not.

explanations.art: A dress shown in a middle strip with blue-and-black on one side and white-and-gold on the other, and two children looking at it with different thought bubbles.
explanations.context: This card is about a photo that people still argue about, and what it shows about colour and the brain.

explanations.concept: Seeing differently, or seeing different things?
explanations.description: Two people look at the same red apple. Are they having the same experience? Nobody has a way to check. Everyone has learned to call that colour red, so everyone says red. In 1689, the English thinker John Locke asked whether one person's blue might be another's yellow without anyone ever knowing. Today we can measure colour sensors and compare the nerve signals of different people. Most people have the same three kinds of colour sensor, so the signals are likely to be similar. But what the signals feel like from the inside cannot be measured from the outside. Thinkers call this the problem of other minds. Their word for what an experience feels like from the inside is qualia.
examples: A person with red-green colour blindness sees some colours differently from most people, and they learn this only by testing.
A bee and a child look at a flower and see different patterns.
Two friends taste the same mango, and one says it is very sweet and one says it is only a little sweet.

perspectives.explanation: People have the same body parts, and the same brain layout. Their experiences are probably very much alike, even if we cannot prove it.
An experience is private. We can compare what people say, and what their nerves do, but not what the experience is like. We cannot rule out differences.

explanations.art: Two children looking at the same red apple, each with a thought bubble that is blank, and a question mark between them.
explanations.context: This card is about a question nobody can yet answer: whether we all see the same thing.

explanations.concept: Time in your head: a minute is not always a minute
explanations.definition: How long a stretch of time feels depends on how much attention you give to time itself. When you attend to the clock, it feels longer. When you are busy, it feels shorter.
explanations.description: A waiting minute can feel very long, and a minute of a good game can feel short. Scientists who study this think that the brain has an inner clock that gives out beats, and that the brain counts the beats. Attention decides how many beats get counted. When you are watching the clock, many beats are counted and the time feels long. When your attention is on a task, fewer beats are counted and the time feels short. Tests in which people tell when a minute has passed show this pattern on average, but it is a small effect and varies between people. Scientists still argue about how the brain tells time, and there may be more than one inner clock.
examples: The last five minutes before the school bell feel very long.
An hour of your favourite game feels very short.
The wait in the dentist's waiting room feels longer than the time with the dentist.
explanations.art: Two clocks side by side with the same time, one drawn stretched long for a child waiting, and one drawn short for a child playing.
explanations.context: This card is about whether the time we feel is the same as the time on the clock.

agreed.text: A drawing that fits two readings is seen as one reading at a time, and the brain flips between them without the viewer choosing.
agreed.evidence: The Necker cube has been tested since 1832 on people of every age. Brain scans show activity changing at each flip, while the drawing on the page stays exactly the same.

agreed.text: Detailed seeing needs attention, so people often miss large things that they are not attending to.
agreed.evidence: In the gorilla video, about half of the viewers counting passes did not see the gorilla. In the stranger and the door test, about half did not notice that the person asking directions had been swapped for another.

agreed.text: A change is hard to see when something hides the moment it happens. Without the hiding flash or blink, the same change is noticed at once.
agreed.evidence: Rensink and others showed pairs of photos that differ in one big way. People needed many flashes to find the change, but saw it at once when the flash was removed.

agreed.text: What the brain expects changes what it reads and what it finds, and searching for one kind of thing can hide another.
agreed.evidence: Many readers miss the doubled 'the' in a familiar phrase. Chicks that had been finding one type of grain were slower to find a second type.

agreed.text: The brain groups bits into wholes and can show edges that are not there.
agreed.evidence: Most people see a white triangle in the ghost triangle drawing. Nerve cells in the visual part of a monkey's brain responded to those missing edges as if they were drawn.

agreed.text: Upright faces are read in a special way, and are harder to recognise upside down.
agreed.evidence: In 1969 Robert Yin found that turning a face upside down makes it much harder to recognise, more than it does for other objects. The Thatcher effect shows it clearly: a face with its eyes and mouth turned upside down looks horrible upright and almost normal upside down.

agreed.text: Camouflage works by fooling the way a hunter's brain reads a scene, by matching the background or by breaking up the outline.
agreed.evidence: In field tests with paper moths on tree trunks, birds found moths with outline-breaking patterns less often than moths without them.

challenging.claim: The eye works like a camera and records the world exactly as it is.
challenging.who: Many people before the 1800s. It is still a common idea in school.
challenging.for: The eye has a lens and a screen, the retina, like a camera.
challenging.against: A camera records whatever it is pointed at. The brain picks. The same lines can be read two ways, big changes can go unseen, and what you expect changes what you see.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that seeing is like taking a photograph.

challenging.claim: If something is right in front of you, you will see it.
challenging.who: Almost everyone, until they are tested.
challenging.for: The light from the thing reaches your eye, so it feels as if it must be seen.
challenging.against: About half of the people counting passes missed a gorilla that walked across the screen. Without attention, large things can be missed.
challenging.context: This card is about whether looking at something means seeing it.

challenging.claim: People who miss the gorilla, or a change, are careless or have poor eyesight.
challenging.who: Many people, when they miss something they are told is obvious.
challenging.for: Once someone points it out, it looks very obvious.
challenging.against: People with good eyesight and a lot of experience miss such things too. Missing them is how the brain normally deals with a limited amount of attention.
challenging.context: This card is about whether missing things shows carelessness.

challenging.claim: Everyone sees colours in the same way.
challenging.for: Most people have the same three kinds of colour sensor and agree on names such as red.
challenging.against: A photo of a dress was seen by some as blue and black and by others as white and gold. People with colour blindness see some colours differently. Nobody can compare what the colour feels like inside.
challenging.context: This card is about whether colour looks the same to everyone.

challenging.claim: If you try hard enough, you can see everything in a scene.
challenging.for: Trying hard to look can make you notice more.
challenging.against: Attention is limited. Looking harder at one thing makes you notice less about other things. You can train what you look for, but not see everything at once.
challenging.context: This card is about whether trying harder can make you see all of a scene.

challenging.claim: Seeing faces in clouds and walls is a mistake the brain should not make.
challenging.who: Some people, who think it is silly.
challenging.for: There is no face in a socket or a cloud.
challenging.against: The brain's face detector is set to respond even to a rough match, because missing a real face matters much more than being fooled now and then. The skill that finds faces in clouds is the same one that finds friends in a crowd.
challenging.context: This card is about whether pareidolia is a fault or a useful habit.

big_questions.q: A cube drawing flips by itself, and you cannot see both readings at once. The paper never changes. So where does the flip happen?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is on the paper, and what your brain does with it.

big_questions.q: In the Blink Tray, watchers looked straight at a tray while a big red cup came and went, and they did not see it. If you can look at something and miss it, what does it mean to see?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between light entering the eye and the brain noticing.

big_questions.q: You and your friend look at the same photo of a dress. You see blue and black, and she sees white and gold. Are you seeing differently, or seeing different things?
big_questions.hint: Think about the same photo, the same light, and two brains making different guesses about the light.

big_questions.q: A bee sees stripes on a flower that looks plain to you. Is the flower striped or plain?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is on the flower, and what is in the eyes of whoever looks at it.

big_questions.q: A face appears in a wall socket. Is the face in the wall, in your brain, or somewhere between them?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the wall provides and what your brain adds.

big_questions.q: Your brain never shows you 'maybe'. When do people decide too early what a person or a situation is like? How could you keep a second reading in mind for longer?
big_questions.hint: Think about the cube: it was easy to see one reading, and hard to hold two.

big_questions.q: Attention is limited. So what might be happening in this room right now that you are not seeing?
big_questions.hint: Think about the gorilla that viewers missed, the change on the tray, and the doubled word in 'Paris in the the spring'.

big_questions.q: A minute of waiting feels long, and a minute of playing feels short. Which one is the real minute?
big_questions.hint: Think about the clock on the wall, and the clock in the head.

big_questions.q: Nobody can step inside another person to compare their red with yours. How could you ever find out whether it is the same?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you can compare, such as what people say and what their nerves do, and what you cannot.

story.title: The Leaf That Was Not a Leaf
story.note: The story is made up, and the people in it are not real. The science is real. Leaf insects live in forests in India, among them the Western Ghats and the North-East, and eat leaves such as guava. Luuk Tinbergen suggested search images in 1960, and Marian Dawkins reported tests with young chicks in 1971. In real life, a leaf insect would be handled only by trained people and put back where she was found.
text: Sowmya's grandfather had been a forest guard for forty years, and he had one boast. "In all my years," Thatha liked to say, "no creature has ever hidden from me."

He said it at breakfast. He said it to the postman. He said it once to a cow. So when Leela Chithi, Sowmya's aunt, came home from the insect research station in the hills and heard the boast, she smiled in a way that Sowmya knew meant trouble.

"Thatha," said Chithi, "tomorrow morning there will be a creature on the guava bush by your veranda. If you can find her in one minute, I will carry your umbrella for a month. If you cannot, you will carry mine."
"Done," said Thatha, and he shook her hand so hard that her bangles rang.

In the morning the rain had stopped, and every leaf on the guava bush was dripping and shining. Thatha stood in front of the bush in his old khaki cap. He took off his glasses, wiped them, and put them on again.
"One minute," said Chithi, pressing a button on her phone.

Thatha was very good at looking. He looked low, and then high. He looked for movement. He looked for the glint of an eye. He found a snail. He found two ants, a tiny spider, and a caterpillar the size of a grain of rice. Each time he cried, "Is that her?" and each time Chithi said, "No."
"Time," said Chithi at last.
Thatha's moustache drooped. "There is nothing on that bush," he said. "You are cheating."

Sowmya had been sitting on the step with a plate of idli. She was nine, and her eyes were not as sharp as Thatha's. But she had a habit that he did not have. When she could not find something, she asked herself what she was looking for.
"Thatha," she said, "what exactly were you looking for?"
"A creature," he said. "A bug. Something with legs, sitting on a leaf."
"That is it," said Sowmya. "You were looking for something sitting on a leaf. What if she is not sitting on a leaf?"
"Then where?"
"What if she is the leaf?"
Thatha opened his mouth, and closed it. He looked at the bush again. There were hundreds of leaves, all green, all veined, all shining with rain. "How do I find one leaf among hundreds?"
"Do not look for a creature," said Sowmya. "Look for a leaf that is wrong."
"Wrong how?"
"Too flat. Too neat. Or with a bite mark that is not like the other bite marks."

So Thatha looked in a way he had not looked in forty years. He did not look for a bug. He looked at every leaf as if it were a suspect. And at last, near his own shoulder, his eyes stopped on one leaf that was just like the others, except for a small brown patch at one edge, like a bite. A breeze came, and every leaf trembled. This leaf swayed to and fro, softly, a little longer than the rest, as if she were not quite sure that she was a leaf.
"Her?" he whispered.
"Her," said Leela Chithi.

Close up, the leaf had a stalk, and veins, and a ragged brown edge. It also had six thin legs, flattened and folded into the shape of leaf pieces, and a small head tucked under one edge. She was a leaf insect, one of the animals who spend their whole lives pretending to be leaves.
Thatha stared for a long time. "Forty years in the forest," he said at last, "and I looked at her a dozen times."

"You did," said Chithi. "You looked straight at her, again and again. You just did not see her, because you were looking for a bug, and she is not one. Birds have the same trouble. A bird that has eaten ten green caterpillars goes on looking for green caterpillars, and a brown one can walk right under her beak."
"And you, Thatha," said Sowmya, "were looking for what you expected."
"My granddaughter," said Thatha, "has been listening to too many scientists." But he was smiling.

That evening, Thatha carried Leela Chithi's umbrella, though it was not raining. He carried it the next day too, and the next. He carried it to the temple, the market and the post office. And whenever anyone asked him why, he said, "I am proud to carry it. My granddaughter found the creature that I was too clever to find."

As for the leaf insect, Chithi carried her back to the station in her box, and put her on her own guava bush. For the rest of that month, whenever Sowmya looked at a bush, she did not look for a bug. She looked for a leaf that was wrong.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the brain finds things faster when it knows what to look for, and it misses things that do not match. A guard who looks for a bug on a leaf can pass a leaf insect many times, because the insect is shaped like the leaf. A mental picture of what to look for is called a search image. Luuk Tinbergen suggested it in 1960, and Marian Dawkins reported in 1971 that chicks used to one type of grain were slower to find another. Camouflage works because it fits what a hunter expects.
ask: Why did a forest guard with sharp eyes fail to find the leaf insect for a whole minute?
What is the difference between looking for a bug on a leaf and looking for a leaf that is wrong?
What is a search image, and how could you use one to find a lost key faster?
Why might a hunter that has been eating one kind of prey walk past a different kind?

games.title: What Does the Word Mean to Me?
games.context: This is a drawing game. Everyone hears the same word and draws the first thing that comes into their head. Then you look at how different the drawings are.

printables.title: Team score sheet
items: Number of different kinds of drawing

rules: Cut out the 24 word cards. Shuffle them and stack them face down. Every player has a small piece of paper and a pencil.
One player turns up the top card and reads the word aloud. Nobody talks after that.
Everyone draws the very first thing that comes into their head when they hear the word. You have 20 seconds. A quick sketch is enough.
Hold the drawings up together. As a team, sort the drawings into piles of the same kind of thing.
The team scores 1 point for each different pile. The aim is to find as many different kinds as you can, so a surprise is a good thing.
Each player says in one sentence why that drawing came to mind. Then the player whose drawing is the only one of its kind gets a star.
Play 12 cards. The team wins if it scores at least 9 points for each player (18 points for 2 players, 36 for 4). If you score less, play again with new cards and try to beat your score.
Playing alone, draw each word now. Draw it again tomorrow without looking at the first drawing. Then compare the two.

flow.do: Cut out the word cards. Shuffle them and stack them face down. Give every player a piece of paper and a pencil.
flow.say: I will read a word. You draw the first thing you think of, in 20 seconds. Do not talk and do not peek at anyone's paper.
flow.kid: Cut out the word cards. Get a pencil and paper. Do not peek.
flow.context: This is the first step of What Does the Word Mean to Me? You set up the cards and learn the rules.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, sort the drawings into piles and count the piles. Ask each player why they drew what they did.
flow.say: Hold up your drawings together. Which drawings show the same kind of thing? How many different piles do we have? Why did you draw that?
flow.kid: Hold up your drawing. Which drawings are alike? Say why you drew yours.

ask.q: Why do you think everyone drew something different for the same word?
good: We each have different memories of that word.
The word can mean many things.
The first thing you think of depends on where you live and what you do.

flow.parent: A word like HOME may give a house, a family, a kitchen or a village. A word like ROUND may give a ball, a roti, a moon or a bangle. Do not say any drawing is wrong.
flow.context: In this step, you play six cards and count the different kinds of drawing.

flow.do: Play the next six cards in the same way. Add up the team's score. Notice which words gave the most different drawings and which gave the fewest.
flow.say: Which words gave us the most different drawings? Which gave the fewest? What do you notice about the two kinds of word?
flow.kid: Play six more cards. Which word gave the most different drawings?
flow.parent: Often, words for one clear thing, such as ROUND, give fewer kinds of drawing than words with wide meanings, such as HOME or SAFE. If your results differ, write them down as they are.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the cards and compare which words gave the most different drawings.

flow.do: Add up the score. Ask the closing question and the check.
flow.say: We all heard the same word. Did we all think of the same thing? What does that tell you about what the word 'means'?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Did you all think of the same thing?

check.q: Four friends hear the word 'HOME'. They draw four different things. What is the best explanation?
options: Each friend's brain reads the word using their own memories and expectations
Three friends were not listening
The word has only one correct meaning
check.why: The same word gives the brain only a clue. The brain fills in the rest from memories of homes it has known. Four brains with four sets of memories give four drawings. Nobody was wrong, and a word does not have just one meaning.

flow.context: In this step, you add up the points and think about why the drawings differed.

games.title: Two Readings: the sentence that fools your brain
games.context: This is a word game. Each sentence can be read in more than one way. You say the first meaning that came to you, and then hunt for the second one.

printables.title: 12 sentence cards: the sentence on the front, the readings on the back

items.b: Reading 1: I saw her pet duck. Reading 2: I saw her bend down quickly.

items.f: She hit the boy with the umbrella.
items.b: Reading 1: She used an umbrella to hit him. Reading 2: She hit the boy who was holding the umbrella.

items.f: Meena saw the girl with the binoculars.
items.b: Reading 1: Meena used binoculars to see the girl. Reading 2: The girl was the one holding the binoculars.
Without a comma, it sounds as if Paati is the food. With a comma, 'Let's eat, Paati!' means let us eat together. One comma changes the reading.

items.f: The chicken is ready to eat.
items.b: Reading 1: The cooked chicken is ready to be eaten. Reading 2: The live chicken is hungry and ready to have her own food.
Reading 1: Going to visit relatives is tiring. Reading 2: Relatives who come to visit us are tiring.
Reading 1: Flying a plane can be dangerous. Reading 2: Planes that are flying can be dangerous.

Read 'the old' as 'old people' and 'man' as an action: to be the crew of a boat. Old people are the crew of the boat. Most readers first take 'the old man' as one person, and then the sentence stops making sense.

items.f: Time flies like an arrow. Fruit flies like a banana.
items.b: In the first sentence, 'flies' is something time does. In the second, 'fruit flies' are insects and 'like' means 'enjoy'. The same words change their jobs.

items.f: Tara told Anitha that she was brilliant.
items.b: 'She' could be Tara or Anitha. The sentence does not say, so readers guess from what they expect.
Reading 1: the edge of a river. Reading 2: a place that keeps money.

rules: Cut out the 12 sentence cards. Stack them with the sentence side up. The back stays hidden.
One player is the reader. The reader reads the top sentence aloud, slowly, and keeps the back hidden.
Everyone says aloud, at the same moment, the first meaning that came into their head.
Now everyone hunts for a second meaning. The first player to say a second meaning that makes sense scores 2 points.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. A player who found a different good meaning that is not on the back also scores 2 points.
The reader job passes to the next player after every card. After all 12 cards, the player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
Playing alone, say the first meaning aloud, then write it down. Hunt for a second meaning. Then turn the card over and check. Score 1 point for each second meaning you find.

flow.do: Cut out the sentence cards and stack them with the sentence side up. Choose the first reader.
flow.say: Each sentence has more than one meaning. First, say the meaning that came to you. Then hunt for another.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Choose who reads first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Readings. You set up the cards.

flow.do: Play the first four cards. After each, ask the players which meaning came first, and how long it took to find the second.
flow.say: Say your first meaning now. Now hunt for another one. How long did it take to find it?
flow.kid: Say your first meaning. Then hunt for another one.

ask.q: Why did the second meaning take longer than the first?
good: My brain chose the first one and stopped looking.
The first one popped into my head at once.
I could only think of one meaning at a time.

flow.parent: Many people find that the second meaning needs a pause. That pause is the point: the brain picks one reading at once, and the other takes effort to find.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first four sentence cards and notice how quickly the first meaning arrives.

flow.do: Play the other eight cards. Keep a tally of points. Notice which sentences were the hardest to read in a second way.
flow.say: Keep going. Which sentence was the hardest to read in a second way? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Play the other cards. Which sentence was the hardest?
flow.parent: 'The old man the boat' is the hardest for most people. The sentence stops making sense halfway, and the reader has to go back and start again.
flow.context: In this step, you play the rest of the cards and notice which sentences are hardest.

flow.do: Add up the scores. Ask the closing question and the check.
flow.say: Add up your points. In the cube drawing, the brain flipped between two readings. What did your brain do with the sentences?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which sentence was hardest?

check.q: Why do most people find 'The old man the boat' hard to read?
options: The brain picks a likely reading, 'the old man', and has to go back when it does not fit
The words are too long
The sentence has no verb in any reading
check.why: The brain reads one word at a time and guesses ahead. It takes 'the old man' as one person. When the next words do not fit, it has to give up that reading and start again. The words are short, and the sentence does have a verb, 'man'.

flow.context: In this step, you add up the scores and explain why one sentence was so hard to read.

experiments.title: Count the Flips: one cube drawing, two readings
experiments.question: How many times does a cube drawing flip in one minute? Can you hold it to one reading by trying? Does it flip at different rates for different people?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many times will the cube flip in one minute? Will trying to hold it still make it flip less, the same or more? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every person looks at the same drawing, at arm's length, in the same light, for exactly 60 seconds. You say the same words to every person. Half of the people start with just watching and half start with trying to hold one reading, so that practice does not help one test more than the other. Nobody taps or counts in their head. Only what the person tries to do changes.
results_table: Flips in 60 seconds, trying to hold one reading
What it felt like, in their own words

materials.item: a sheet of plain white paper
a ruler and a black pen
a phone with a stopwatch
a pencil and a sheet of paper for the helper who tallies each flip (the other child, or the parent)
one to three other people who agree to try, such as a parent, a brother or sister, or a friend (a parent and one child can do the whole test; more people make the comparison better)
a table and chair in a well-lit place

schedule.what: Draw the cube, test yourself twice with just watching and once trying to hold it, then test three other people and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each person, add the two just-watching counts and divide by two. Draw a bar for each person's average, and a mark for their trying-to-hold count.

flow.do: Show your child a cube drawing in a book, or draw a quick one. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: I will draw a cube with lines. You will look at it for one minute. Will the cube stay the same? Will it change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will look at a cube made of lines for one minute. Will it stay the same? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a drawing that does not change might look different?
good: My eyes might get tired.
It could look like a cube from the front or from the back.
My brain might change its mind.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Many children guess that it will not change.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Flips. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Draw a square 5 centimetres wide with the ruler. 2. Draw a second square of the same size, starting 2 centimetres to the right and 2 centimetres up. The squares overlap. 3. Join each corner of the first square to the matching corner of the second with a straight line. 4. Go over the lines with the black pen.
flow.say: Draw one square. Draw a second square of the same size, a little up and to the right. Now join the four matching corners with straight lines.
flow.kid: Draw a square. Draw a second, up and to the right. Join the corners.
flow.parent: The twelve lines must all show, with no hidden lines. If you prefer, copy the cube from a book. Place the drawing flat on the table at arm's length from your child.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the cube that you will watch.

flow.do: Test your child, just watching. Say: look at the cube for one minute. Every time it seems to flip so that a different corner comes forward, say flip. Start the stopwatch, and make a mark each time. Do it twice, with a short rest between.
flow.say: Look at the cube. Keep your eyes on it. Every time it flips, say flip. I will count. Ready, go.
flow.kid: Look at the cube for one minute. Say flip each time it changes.
flow.parent: If there is no flip after 30 seconds, say: let your eyes drift to another corner. Or blink slowly. Some people take a while to see the first flip. Write down the number even if it is 0.
flow.context: In this step, your child watches the cube for a minute, twice, and says flip each time it changes.

flow.do: Now test your child while they try to hold one reading. Say: pick one reading and keep it for the whole minute. If it flips, say flip, and try to bring it back. Start the stopwatch and make a mark for each flip.
flow.say: Now choose one way to see the cube. Try hard to keep it that way for one minute. If it flips anyway, say flip, and bring it back.
flow.kid: Pick one way to see the cube. Try to keep it for a minute.
flow.parent: Most people find that trying slows the flips down, but few can stop them. Write down what your child says it feels like. Do not tell them what you expect.
flow.context: In this step, your child tries to hold the cube in one reading for a minute.

flow.do: Test the three other people in the same way: one minute just watching, and one minute trying to hold one reading. Half of the people do the trying test first. Write every number in the table.
flow.say: Now let us test other people. Same drawing, same words, same one minute. Let us see if the cube flips the same number of times for everyone.
flow.kid: Test three more people. Same words, same minute. Write down how many flips each one saw.
flow.parent: Use the same words every time. Do not show anyone how it flips. Some people will say it never flips. Ask them once to let their eyes drift to another corner, or to blink slowly. If they still see no flip in two minutes, write 0: that is a result too. You can also make the cube bigger with thicker lines. With two to four children, pair up: one child looks while another tallies and holds the stopwatch, then they swap, so every child is tested. About 3 to 20 flips a minute is typical, and it varies a lot between people.
flow.context: In this step, you test three other people with the same drawing.

flow.do: Compare the numbers. Ask your child what they think is true, which numbers show it, and why it happens. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Did the cube flip the same number of times for everyone? Did trying to hold it change the number? What do you think is happening, if the lines never change?
flow.kid: Did the cube flip the same number of times for everyone? Did trying to hold it change the number?
flow.parent: Common results are that most people see several flips a minute, that trying slows the flips for many people, and that people differ a lot. Your results may differ. If one reading was seen far more than the other, write it down.

check.q: Why does a cube drawing flip, though the lines on the paper never change?
options: The lines fit two cubes equally well, and the brain switches between them
The paper moves a little each time
The eyes see double and then see single
check.why: The lines could be a cube pointing one way or the other, and both readings fit. The brain can show only one reading at a time, and it switches between them. The paper does not move, and the eyes are not seeing double.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the results and explain why the cube flips.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you count how often a cube drawing flips in one minute, and find out whether trying can stop it.

experiments.title: The Blink Tray: how long does a big change stay unseen?
experiments.question: A card covers a tray for a moment, and one thing on the tray changes while it is covered. Each cover is called a blink. How many blinks does it take a watcher to notice the change? Is a big thing in the middle found sooner than a small thing at the edge?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Each time the card covers the tray is one blink. How many blinks will it take a watcher to find a big red cup that appears and disappears? Will a small button at the edge take more or fewer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every watcher sees the same tray with the same ten things. The card covers the tray for about one second each time, and the tray is in view for about three seconds. The same person holds the card and the same person changes the thing each time. The only difference between the two tests is which thing changes: the big red cup in the middle, or the small button at the edge. You move the other things between tests so that a watcher will not recall where they were.
results_table: Blinks to find the big red cup in the middle
Blinks to find the small button at the edge
Did the watcher see it at once when the cup was taken away in plain sight? (yes or no)

materials.item: a large tray, a big plate or a table mat

ten small different things from the house, including a big red plastic cup and a small button, and others such as a steel spoon, a comb, a pencil, an eraser, a bangle, a hair clip and a steel katori (no sharp things)
a big stiff card or a folded newspaper board, large enough to cover the whole tray

up to three watchers who do not know which thing will change (parent, grandparent, sibling or neighbour). With only one child and one parent, take turns: one is the watcher while the other changes the tray, and then swap
a chair for each watcher, and a table
paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.safety: Keep small things such as buttons and bangles away from children under five, who might put them in their mouths.

schedule.what: Practise covering the tray with the card, with no watcher. Then test three watchers, each with the big change and the small change.

experiments.record: For each watcher, write how many blinks it took to find each change, up to 15. Add the numbers for the big change and for the small change. Draw two bars.

flow.do: Show your child the tray and the ten things. Explain that a card will cover the tray for a moment, and a thing will change. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: A card will cover the tray for a second. Under the card, one thing will come or go. Do you think the watcher will see it at once? Why?
flow.kid: A card hides the tray for a second. One thing changes. Will you see it at once?

ask.q: Why do you think people might miss a big change when a card hides it for a second?
good: I would be looking at something else.
My eyes would not see the change happen.
My brain would not compare the before and after.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many people say that they would see it at once, and that is a good guess to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blink Tray test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Practise with no watcher. One person holds the card flat over the tray for about one second and lifts it away for about three seconds. The other person puts the red cup on the tray or takes it away while the card is down. Practise until it is smooth and silent.
flow.say: Cover the tray, count one, and lift the card. While the card is down, I will take the cup away or put it back. Then we count one, two, three, and cover again.
flow.kid: Cover the tray for one second. Lift the card. Count to three. Cover again.
flow.parent: The change must happen only while the card is down, and silently. Keep the other things still. A smooth rhythm is the key. If the card moves slowly, the watcher can see the cup move. One person can do both jobs with one hand holding the card over the tray and the other hand reaching underneath, so a child and a parent can work alone. With 2 to 4 children, one holds the card, one changes the tray, one is the watcher and one counts and writes; rotate the jobs.
flow.context: In this step, you practise covering and uncovering the tray with no watcher, so the test is smooth.

flow.do: Bring in one watcher and sit them at the table. First, show a change in plain sight: with no card, take the red cup away slowly while the watcher watches the tray. Ask what changed. Write yes or no for noticing at once.
flow.say: Watch the tray, please. I will take something away now. What changed? That was easy. Now, with the card, we will see if it is still easy.
flow.kid: Watch the tray. Something will change in plain sight. Can you see it?
flow.parent: Do this with each watcher before their blink tests. In plain sight, almost everyone sees the change at once, because they see it move. This is the control, the test you compare the others with. It shows that the change is easy to see when the card is not hiding it.
flow.context: In this step, you show a watcher that a change in plain sight is easy to see.

flow.do: Test the watcher with the blink. Test 1: the red cup comes and goes at each blink. Count the blinks until the watcher says what changed. Stop at 15. Move the other things to new places. Test 2: the button at the edge comes and goes at each blink. Count the blinks. Test two more watchers, and swap which test goes first.
flow.say: Now we will use the card. After each blink, tell me if you see a change and what it is. I will count the blinks. Ready?
flow.kid: Watch the tray. After each blink, say what changed. Count the blinks.
flow.parent: Write down the number of blinks. If the watcher guesses wrongly, say no and carry on. Give each watcher the tests in a different order. People who find the cup quickly may take more blinks for the button, and some people find both at once. If every watcher sees the change on the very first blink, the scene is too easy: add four or five more things to the tray, or shorten the time the tray is in view to about two seconds. If nobody sees it by blink 15, stop and say so. That is a real result, and it shows how hard this is. Typical results are a few blinks for the big red cup and more for the small button, but yours may differ.
flow.context: In this step, you test three watchers with a big change and a small change.

flow.do: Add up the blinks for the big change and the small change. Draw two bars. Ask your child what they think is true, which numbers show it, and why it happens. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which change took more blinks? Was the plain-sight change easy? What was different when the card was down?
flow.kid: Add up the blinks. Which change took more? Why?

check.q: A big change in a tray goes unseen when a card covers the moment of change. What is the best explanation?
options: The brain does not see the change happen, and it compares before and after only in the place it is attending to
The watcher's eyes were closed
The red cup was too small to see
check.why: In plain sight the brain sees the thing move, and that catches attention at once. When the card hides the moment of change, there is no movement to see, and the brain has to compare two scenes. It does that only for the few things it is attending to. The eyes were open, and the cup was large.

flow.context: In this step, you add up the blinks and explain why a big change can go unseen.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you hide the moment of change in a tray with a card, and count how many blinks it takes for a watcher to find it.

experiments.title: Upside-Down Faces: which looks stranger?
experiments.question: If the eyes and mouth in a face are turned upside down, does the face look strange? Does it look equally strange when the whole face is upside down?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. A face has its eyes and mouth turned upside down. How strange will it look when the whole face is upright? How strange will it look when the whole face is upside down? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every rater sees the same four cards for exactly three seconds each, in the same light, and answers the same question: how strange does the face look, from 0 for normal to 5 for very strange. The two upside-down cards are always shown first, so that no rater has seen the changed face upright before rating the upside-down cards. This order is not perfect, but it keeps the changed face from being given away. Only the card changes.

materials.item: two copies of the same clear photo of a face looking straight ahead, each at least 10 centimetres tall. Print one photo twice at a photo or cyber shop (about Rs 5 to 10 each), or photocopy a page at a stationery shop (about Rs 2). Use someone who agrees
scissors, used by a grown-up
glue stick or tape, and two pieces of card as big as the photos (an old cereal or biscuit box will do)
a phone with a stopwatch, to time three seconds for each card
three to five people who agree to be raters and have not seen the cards
paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with the scissors. Ask the person in the photo before you use it, and do not post the cards or the photos online.

schedule.what: Make the normal card and the changed card, then show four cards to five raters and write their scores.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out the average score of the raters for each of the four cards. Draw four bars.

flow.do: Show your child a photo of a face. Explain that you will turn the eyes and the mouth upside down inside the face. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We will turn the eyes and the mouth of a face upside down. Will the face look strange? Will it look equally strange upside down? Why?
flow.kid: We will flip a face's eyes and mouth. Will it look strange? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a face might look strange upright but not upside down?
good: Because I am used to seeing faces upright.
Because upside down I look at the parts, not the whole face.
It will look strange both ways, because the eyes are wrong.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess that the changed face will look strange in both positions, and that is a good guess to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Upside-Down Faces test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Stick the normal photo on a card. This is the normal face. 2. On the second photo, a grown-up cuts out a strip across both eyes and eyebrows, and a patch across the mouth. Keep the two cut pieces. 3. Stick the second photo, with its two holes, on the second card. 4. Turn both pieces upside down and glue them into their holes on the card.
flow.say: Stick one photo on a card. This is the normal one. On the other photo, a grown-up cuts out the eyes and the mouth. Turn each piece upside down and stick it back.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts out the eyes and mouth. Turn them upside down. Stick them back.
flow.parent: A clear photo of a face looking straight ahead works best. A drawing gives a weaker effect. Cut slightly outside the eyebrows and the lips so the pieces fit back well, and keep the pieces large, as small ones are hard to turn and glue. With 2 to 4 children, each child can make a card pair from a different photo, and the raters compare them.
flow.context: In this step, you make the normal card and the changed card.

flow.do: Show each rater four cards, one at a time, for three seconds each, timed with the phone. The order is: normal upside down, changed upside down, normal upright, changed upright. After each card, ask how strange the face looks, from 0 to 5. Write the numbers.
flow.say: I will show you a face for three seconds. Then tell me how strange it looks. Zero is normal and five is very strange. Do not look for long.
flow.kid: Show a face for three seconds. Ask how strange it looks, from 0 to 5.
flow.parent: Show the upside-down cards first, with the card held upside down. Do not say what you changed. Some raters will say the changed upright face looks horrible, and that is the main result. With fewer than five people, three raters are enough; the pattern shows with a few. The children can take turns to hold the card, time three seconds and write the score.
flow.context: In this step, you show the four cards to five raters and write their scores.

flow.do: Work out the average score for each card. Draw four bars. Ask your child what they think is true, which numbers show it, and why it happens. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Which card has the highest average? Is the changed face much stranger upright or upside down? What does that tell you about how we read faces?
flow.kid: Find the average for each card. Draw four bars. Which is highest?
flow.parent: A common result is that the changed face looks much stranger upright than upside down, even though it is the same photo. Your results may differ. If the changed face looks equally odd in both, write that down.

check.q: A face with its eyes and mouth turned upside down looks horrible upright, but almost normal upside down. What does this show?
options: The brain reads an upright face as a whole, and the oddness of its parts shows up only when it is upright
The eyes and mouth look normal upside down in every case
The brain cannot see upside-down faces at all
check.why: When a face is upright, the brain reads all the parts together as one face and notices that something is wrong. When the face is upside down, it reads the parts one by one, and the changed parts do not stand out. The brain can see upside-down faces, but less well.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the averages and explain what the cards show about faces.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you turn the eyes and the mouth of a photo upside down, and ask people how strange it looks upright and upside down.
