activities.title: Count the F's, and Spot the Extra Word

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a thick pen
two or more people who have not seen the sentence (the child, plus a parent, a brother or sister, or a friend)
a phone with a stopwatch
a pencil and a table for the results

schedule.what: Ask people to count the letter F in a sentence, and to read three lines that each hide a doubled word.

activities.record: A table with a row for each person. Write how many F's they found, and whether they noticed the doubled word in each of the three lines.
activities.context: In this activity, you ask people to count letters in a sentence and to read three short lines, and you find out what they miss.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with the sentence about finished files written in big capital letters, and a pen beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Write the sentence in big capital letters on a sheet of paper.

setup.art: A grown-up reading the sheet with a finger on her lip, and a child holding up a phone stopwatch showing 15 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Give each person 15 seconds to count the letter F, without pointing.

setup.art: Three lines of text with a repeated word in each, and a child looking at a person's face as they read aloud.
setup.caption: 3. Ask each person to read three lines aloud, and watch what they say.

flow.do: Write this sentence in big capital letters. FINISHED FILES ARE THE RESULT OF YEARS OF SCIENTIFIC STUDY COMBINED WITH THE EXPERIENCE OF YEARS. Ask your child to count the letter F in 15 seconds, silently, without pointing. Ask for a guess about how many.
flow.say: Count the letter F in this sentence. Do not point with your finger. You have fifteen seconds. How many do you think there are, and why?
flow.kid: Count every F in the sentence. Do not point. You have 15 seconds.
flow.parent: Write the sentence out in full. Let your child write down the number. Then try the other people. Do not tell anyone the answer yet. Many people find three, and some find four or five.
flow.context: In this step, you ask your child to count the letter F in a sentence.

flow.do: Ask your child to point to each word with a pencil and count the F in each word slowly. There are six in all: in FINISHED, FILES, OF, SCIENTIFIC, OF and OF. Then test two other people with the 15-second count and write what they say.
flow.say: Now point at each word and count the F's slowly. How many now? Where did you miss them? Which little word hides three of them?
flow.kid: Point at each word. Count the F's slowly. How many now?
flow.parent: Most people find they missed the F in the word OF. The brain skips small, common words when it reads for meaning. The F's were there. The eyes saw them, but they were not noticed.
flow.context: In this step, you count slowly, word by word, and find the missing F's.

flow.do: Write three lines on a sheet: A BIRD IN THE THE HAND. PARIS IN THE THE SPRING. LEARN FROM FROM YOUR MISTAKES. Ask each person to read each line aloud once, at normal speed. Write whether each person noticed the doubled word. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Read each line aloud, once, at your normal speed. Do not stop and look again. I am listening for what you say.
flow.kid: Read each line out loud once. Does anything look odd?

check.q: Why do many people miss the doubled word in 'Paris in the the spring'?
options: The brain expects the familiar phrase and skips over the repeat
The words are printed too small
People are not looking at the page
check.why: The brain reads familiar phrases by guessing what comes next, and it does not check every word. It saw 'the' and it expected 'spring', so the repeat went by. The eyes were on the page, and the words were large enough to see.

flow.context: In this step, you ask people to read three lines with a doubled word and see who notices.

activities.title: Vase or Faces? Cut your own two-way picture

materials.item: a sheet of black chart paper, A4 or bigger, or any dark paper (about Rs 10 at a stationery shop; the back of a dark folder also works)
a sheet of white paper, A4 size
a ruler, and a white pencil, chalk or pale crayon to draw on the black paper
scissors, used by a grown-up
three to five people who agree to try

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with the scissors. Keep the cut-off paper strips away from small children.

schedule.what: Cut a vase-and-faces shape from black paper, put it on white paper, and ask five people what they see first and whether they can see both.

activities.record: A table with a row for each person: what they saw first (vase or faces), whether they could see both at once, and how long it took to swap.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a drawing that can be read as a vase or as two faces, and find out how people see it.

setup.art: A sheet of black paper folded in half, with a face profile drawn in white pencil along the edge nearest the open side.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the black paper in half. Draw a face profile near the fold.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting along the profile line and removing a strip between the profile and the fold.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts along the line and removes the strip next to the fold.

setup.art: The black sheet opened out over white paper, showing a white vase shape between two black faces looking at each other.
setup.caption: 3. Open the paper over a white sheet. A vase appears between two faces.

flow.do: Show your child the idea: a drawing in which a vase and two faces share the same edge. Ask for a guess and a reason about whether they can see both at once. Write it down.
flow.say: We will make a drawing in which you might see a vase, or two faces. Do you think you can see both at the same moment? Why?
flow.kid: We will make a drawing with a vase and two faces. Can you see both at once?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If you have a book with a vase-and-faces drawing, show it first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Vase or Faces. You guess before you cut.

flow.do: 1. Fold the black paper in half, short side to short side, with the fold on the left. 2. To the right of the fold, draw the side view of a face looking left, about 2 to 4 centimetres from the fold. 3. Give it a forehead, a nose, lips and a chin. 4. A grown-up cuts along the line and removes the strip next to the fold. 5. Open the paper over the white sheet.
flow.say: Fold the black paper in half. Draw the side of a face near the fold, with a forehead, a nose, lips and a chin. A grown-up will cut it out. Then open it on a white sheet.
flow.kid: Fold the paper. Draw the side of a face near the fold. A grown-up cuts it out.
flow.parent: To draw the outline, mark points about 1 centimetre apart down the page, each measured from the fold in centimetres: the top 3.5, forehead 3, brow 2.2, nose tip 1, under the nose 2, upper lip 1.7, mouth 2.2, lower lip 1.8, chin 2, under the chin 3.2. If your outline does not look like faces, copy a vase-and-faces drawing from a book. Draw on the black paper with a white pencil, chalk or pale crayon, as a normal pencil does not show. When the strip is removed, the paper falls into two halves: lay them on the white sheet with the cut edges facing each other and a small gap, and tape them down. With 2 to 4 children, each child can draw their own face outline and the grown-up cuts them one by one. A wobbly outline is fine. If it does not look like a face, try again with a bigger nose.
flow.context: In this step, you make the two-way picture from black and white paper.

flow.do: Show the picture to five people one at a time. Ask: what do you see first? Then ask: can you see something else? Can you see both at once? Write each answer. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at this. What do you see first? Now, can you see something else? Can you see both at the same time?
flow.kid: Show the drawing to five people. Ask what they see first.
flow.parent: Most people see one reading first, and some need a hint to find the other. Almost nobody sees both at the same moment. People may differ in what they see first, and that is a result.

check.q: In the vase and faces picture, what happens to the vase when you see the faces?
options: The vase becomes the background behind the faces
The vase gets smaller
The vase disappears from the paper
check.why: The brain decides which part is the figure, the thing in front, and which is the ground behind it. When the faces are the figure, the vase becomes part of the empty space between them. The paper does not change at all.

flow.context: In this step, you test five people and note what they see first and whether they can see both.

activities.title: The Triangle That Isn't There

materials.item: a sheet of white paper
a thick black pen or a black crayon
the bottom of a steel katori or a glass, about 5 to 6 centimetres across, to trace round (a coin is too small to work)
a ruler
three to five people who agree to try
a pencil and paper for the table

schedule.what: Draw three circles with a slice missing, arrange them in a triangle, and ask five people what they see.

activities.record: A table with a row for each person: did they see a triangle, did it look brighter than the paper, and what happened when one circle was covered.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw three black circles with slices missing, and find out whether people see a triangle that is not drawn.

setup.art: Three circles traced round a katori on white paper, at the corners of a large triangle, each filled in black with a wedge left white.
setup.caption: 1. Trace three circles. Colour each black, but leave a wedge white.

setup.art: The three black circles with the white wedges all pointing to the middle, and a faint white triangle seen between them.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the wedges to point to the middle. A white triangle appears.

setup.art: A child's finger covering one circle, and the triangle gone from the picture.
setup.caption: 3. Cover one circle. The triangle goes.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess whether people will see a shape between the circles. Trace around the katori or glass three times, so that the three circles sit at the corners of a triangle. Keep the centres of the circles about 11 centimetres apart. Colour each circle black, but leave a wedge, like a slice of pizza, white in each. Turn each wedge to point to the middle of the triangle.
flow.say: We will draw three circles with slices missing. Do you think people will see a shape in the middle? What shape? Why?
flow.kid: Draw three black circles with a slice missing. Point the slices to the middle.
flow.parent: Each white wedge should be narrow, about one sixth of the circle (60 degrees, narrower than a quarter), so that its two edges run along the sides of the triangle. The edges of the white wedges must line up so that they point to the same middle. Do not tell people what to expect. Colour the circles in fully, with a thick black marker or crayon, so the black is dark. The effect is strongest in good light. A few people do not see the triangle, and that is a result. With several children, each can make one drawing with a different wedge size and compare which works best.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Triangle That Isn't There. You guess and make the drawing.

flow.do: Show the drawing to five people, one at a time, from about an arm's length. Ask what they see in the middle. Ask if the shape looks brighter than the paper around it. Write each answer. Then ask each person to cover one circle with a finger, and say what happens.
flow.say: What do you see in the middle? Does it look brighter or the same as the paper? Now cover one circle with your finger. What happens to the shape?
flow.kid: Show the drawing. Ask what people see in the middle.
flow.parent: Most people see a white triangle with clear edges, which often looks brighter than the paper. When one circle is covered, the triangle disappears. The edges of the triangle are not drawn anywhere on the paper.
flow.context: In this step, you test five people to see whether they find a triangle that is not drawn.

flow.do: Count how many people saw a triangle. Ask your child to show where the triangle's edge is on the paper. Ask the check question.
flow.say: How many people saw the triangle? Where is its edge on the paper? Is the edge drawn anywhere?
flow.kid: Count how many people saw a triangle. Is the edge drawn?

check.q: In the drawing of three circles with slices missing, people see a triangle. Where do the triangle's edges come from?
options: The brain draws them, to join the circles into one shape
They are drawn in very thin pencil
They come from the white paper
check.why: No edges are drawn on the paper. The brain groups the three circles into one shape, and it supplies the missing edges so that the shape makes sense. Nerve cells in the visual part of a monkey's brain have been found to respond to such missing edges as though they were real lines.

flow.context: In this step, you count who saw the triangle and think about where its edges come from.

activities.title: Faces in Things: a hunt around the house

materials.item: paper and a pencil for each person
a phone with a timer
two or more family members who agree to join (a parent and child can do it, but more people give more to compare)
a few things around the house: plug sockets, taps, windows, a scooter or an auto outside

activities.safety: Walk outside only with a grown-up, and stay away from roads and traffic.

schedule.what: Hunt for faces in things for five minutes, compare lists, and draw dots in two arrangements.

activities.record: A list for each person of the things in which they found a face. Count how many each person found, and how many were found by more than one person.
activities.context: In this activity, you hunt for faces in objects that are not faces, and find out which patterns make a face.

setup.art: A plug socket and a switch on a wall that look like a surprised face, with two circles for eyes and a slot for a mouth.
setup.caption: 1. Look for faces in plug sockets, taps, windows and the fronts of vehicles.

setup.art: A page with three dots drawn in two ways: two dots above one, and one dot above two.
setup.caption: 2. Draw three dots two ways. Which looks more like a face?

flow.do: Set a timer for 5 minutes. Everyone walks around the house, and outside, if it is safe, looking for faces in things. Each person writes down or sketches each face. Stop when the timer ends. Count the faces found by each person.
flow.say: In five minutes, how many faces can you find in things that are not faces? Write each one. A face can be two circles and a line.
flow.kid: Find faces in things. Plug sockets, taps and scooters may have them.
flow.parent: Common finds are plug sockets, the front of a scooter or an auto, a tap and a steel tumbler, a window with a lamp and a door, and a burnt chapati. Do not say that any find is wrong. Walk outside only if it is safe.
flow.context: In this step, you hunt for faces in objects for five minutes.

flow.do: Compare the lists. Which things did more than one person find? Which faces did only one person find? Draw three dots, two above one, on a piece of paper. Turn the paper upside down. Which looks more like a face?
flow.say: Which things did two people find? Which did only one find? Now look at these three dots. Two above one, and then turned upside down. Which looks like a face?
flow.kid: Compare your lists. Draw three dots, two above one. Turn the paper upside down. Which way looks like a face?
flow.parent: Two dots above one usually looks like a face, and it looks much less like one when turned upside down. Brain scientists think that our brain looks for a pattern of two eyes above a mouth. Newborn babies have been found to look longer at such patterns.
flow.context: In this step, you compare lists and test the three-dot pattern.

flow.do: Ask the check question. Then talk about why the brain might find faces in things that are not faces.
flow.say: Why do you think the brain finds faces in sockets and clouds? What would happen if it missed a real face?
flow.kid: Why does the brain find faces in sockets and clouds?

check.q: Why does a plug socket sometimes look like a face?
options: The brain's face finder responds to any rough pattern of two eyes above a mouth
The socket is really alive
Everyone has seen that socket before
check.why: The brain's face finder is tuned to respond to a rough pattern, because missing a real face matters much more than being fooled by a socket. The socket is not alive, and the face appears even in sockets that nobody has seen before.

flow.context: In this step, you think about why the brain finds faces in objects.

activities.title: One Room, Four Worlds

materials.item: paper, pencils and crayons
a room with a window and five things in it, such as a cup of warm tea, a flower, a plate of food, a fan and a lamp
a grown-up to read out the facts about each animal. With 2 to 4 children, each child takes one animal and says what she or he would notice, then everybody draws the same thing as a different animal

schedule.what: Choose five things in a room, guess what a dog, a bee and a pit viper would notice about each, then check the facts and draw one.

activities.record: A table with five things down the side and four animals across the top (you, a dog, a bee, a pit viper). Fill in what each would notice most about each thing.
activities.context: In this activity, you imagine one room as four different animals would sense it, and then check your guesses against what scientists know.

setup.art: A table with five things in a room listed down the side and the four animals drawn across the top.
setup.caption: 1. List five things in the room. Draw the table.

setup.art: A girl drawing the room as a dog senses the room, with bright trails of smell rising from the food and the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one thing as an animal would sense that thing.

flow.do: Choose five things in the room. For each one, ask your child to guess what a dog, a bee and a pit viper would notice most. Write the guesses in the table. Add what you notice yourself.
flow.say: A dog, a bee and a pit viper are in this room. For each thing, what would each animal notice most? Smell? Colour? Heat? What do you think?
flow.kid: Pick five things in the room. Guess what a dog, a bee and a pit viper, who is a snake, would notice.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses yet. Let your child fill in all four columns first.
flow.context: In this step, you guess what four different animals would notice in one room.

flow.do: Read the facts aloud. A dog has a far larger part of the brain for smell than we have, and sees fewer colours than we do. A honeybee sees ultraviolet light, which we cannot see, and sees red as very dark. A pit viper senses the heat of warm things with pits on her face. Change any guesses that the facts show were wrong. Mark them with a star.
flow.say: Here are the facts. The dog smells much more than we do. The bee sees ultraviolet. The pit viper senses heat. Which of your guesses did the facts change?
flow.kid: Listen to the facts. Which of your guesses changed?
flow.parent: For example, a cup of hot tea shows up for a pit viper as a bright warm spot. A flower may have a pattern in ultraviolet that a bee follows to the middle. A plate of food is a strong cloud of smell to a dog. For things such as a fan, a lamp or a window, the facts are less clear, so discuss them.
flow.context: In this step, you check your guesses against what scientists know about each animal.

flow.do: Choose one thing and one animal. Draw the thing the way that animal would sense it. Use colour, lines or clouds to show smell, heat or ultraviolet. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Pick one thing and one animal. Draw how that animal would sense the thing. Show smell with clouds, heat with red, or ultraviolet with stripes.
flow.kid: Pick one thing and one animal. Draw the thing the way that animal senses it.

check.q: A flower looks plain yellow to you. A bee sees a dark pattern on the flower, in ultraviolet. What does this suggest?
options: The flower has more than one appearance, depending on who looks
The bee is imagining the pattern
The flower changes when the bee arrives
check.why: The pattern is really there, in ultraviolet light, but our eyes cannot sense that light. So the flower looks plain to us and patterned to the bee. The bee is not imagining the pattern, and the flower does not change when the bee arrives.

flow.context: In this step, you draw one thing as one animal senses it, and think about what that means.

activities.safety: Hot tea can scald. Use warm tea in a cup that a grown-up carries and places, away from small children, or just talk about a hot cup instead. Leave the fan and the lamp as they are, on or off, and do not touch the lamp.

activities.title: Say It Thirty Times: when a word loses its meaning

materials.item: a common word on a card, such as TUMBLER, CHAIR or RAIN
a phone with a stopwatch
two or more people who agree to try
a pencil and paper for the results

schedule.what: Say a word thirty times as fast as you can, and say what happened to its sound and its meaning.

activities.record: A table with a row for each person: how the word felt after thirty times (the same, odd, or it lost its meaning), and the word used. Also ask each person to rate how strange the word sounds from 0 to 5 after 10 times and after 30 times.
activities.context: In this activity, you say one word again and again, and find out what happens to its sound and its meaning.

setup.art: A child saying the word tumbler aloud with a row of tally marks showing 30, and a steel tumbler beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Say a word aloud thirty times, as fast as you can.

setup.art: The child looking surprised, with a thought bubble of the same word broken into letters.
setup.caption: 2. Notice what happens to the word.

flow.do: Write a common word on a card. Ask your child to guess what will happen to the word if they say it thirty times, and why. Then ask your child to say it aloud thirty times, as fast as they can, while looking at the card. Count with tally marks. Ask what happened to the word.
flow.say: Say this word thirty times, as fast as you can. Before you start, what do you think will happen to the word? Why?
flow.kid: Say the word 30 times, fast. What happens to it?
flow.parent: Many people say the word starts to sound strange, like a collection of sounds, and that the meaning slips away. Some feel nothing. Both are results. The effect is called semantic satiation, and scientists still discuss how strong it is.
flow.context: This is the first step of Say It Thirty Times. Your child says a word again and again.

flow.do: Try with two other people and a different word each. Write down what each person says. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Now ask two other people to try. Use a different word. What do they say happens?
flow.kid: Ask two other people to try. What do they notice?

check.q: A word said thirty times often starts to sound strange. What does this suggest about meaning?
options: The brain builds the meaning of a word each time, and the meaning can fade for a while when the word is repeated
The word has lost its meaning in the dictionary
The ears have stopped working
check.why: A word's meaning is not stuck to its sound. The brain makes the meaning each time it hears or says the word, and repeating the word many times can make this work less well for a while. The word is still in the dictionary, and the ears are fine.

flow.context: In this step, you test two other people and think about what the result means.

activities.title: Is a Minute a Minute? Waiting and playing

materials.item: a phone with a stopwatch, kept hidden from the person being tested
a blank wall to look at, and an absorbing task such as threading beads, colouring a mandala or a maze
two or more people who agree to try (the child and a parent, or brothers and sisters taking turns)
a pencil and paper for the results

schedule.what: Ask each person to say stop when they think a minute has passed, once while waiting and once while busy, and note the true time.

activities.record: A table with a row for each person: the true seconds when they said stop while waiting, and the true seconds when they said stop while busy. Mark with a C if the person admits that they counted.
activities.context: In this activity, you find out whether a minute feels different when you are waiting and when you are busy.

setup.art: A child looking at a blank wall with a phone stopwatch hidden behind her, held by a grown-up.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a blank wall. Say stop when you think a minute has passed.

setup.art: The same child busy threading beads while the grown-up watches the stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Do it again while you are busy with beads, a maze or colouring.

flow.do: Ask each person to guess whether a minute will feel longer when waiting or when busy, and why. Then test one person while waiting. Start the hidden stopwatch. They look at a blank wall and say stop when they think a minute has passed. Do not let them count or tap. Write the true time.
flow.say: Look at the wall. Do not count and do not tap. When you think one minute has passed, say stop. Before we start, do you think a minute will feel long or short?
flow.kid: Look at the wall. Say stop when you think a minute has passed. Do not count.
flow.parent: Children find it hard not to count. If a person says they counted, write C beside the number. A counted result tells you less. Do not tell anyone what you expect to happen. To keep people from counting, ask them to hum a song quietly or say the days of the week in a loop while they wait; keep the same rule for the busy test.
flow.context: This is the first step of Is a Minute a Minute? You test a waiting minute.

flow.do: Test the same person while they do a task that takes all their attention, such as threading beads. Start the hidden stopwatch. They say stop when they think a minute has passed. Write the true time. Repeat for two more people, and swap which test goes first.
flow.say: Now thread the beads. Do not count. When you think a minute has passed, say stop.
flow.kid: Do the task. Say stop when you think a minute has passed.
flow.parent: People often say stop too early when they wait and too late when they are busy, but the effect is small and it varies. Some people show the opposite. This is a result too, and one trial per person is not enough to be sure.

check.q: A person who is busy says stop at 75 seconds, when they think a minute has passed. What does this suggest?
options: The minute felt shorter than it was, because their attention was on the task
The minute felt longer than it was
The stopwatch was wrong
check.why: At 60 seconds they did not yet feel that a minute had gone, so they waited until 75. When the mind is busy, less attention is given to time, and the time feels shorter. A single trial is not proof, but it matches what scientists find on average.

flow.context: In this step, you test a busy minute and think about what the result means.

flow.do: Compare the waiting and the busy numbers. Ask whether the result is the same for every person.
flow.say: Which was longer, the minute while waiting or while busy? Was it the same for everybody? What might change a minute?
flow.kid: Compare the two numbers. Is it the same for everyone?
flow.parent: A pattern that is the same for all three people is more convincing than a pattern for one. If the results are mixed, say so. That is honest science.
flow.context: In this step, you compare the waiting and the busy minutes across people.

projects.title: Blot Gallery: what do people see in a folded blot?

materials.item: six sheets of plain white paper
washable poster paint in two or three colours, or school watercolours. Strong tea, coffee or a little ink mixed with water also gives a good blot
a spoon or an old brush for each colour, and a little water to thin the paint to the thickness of cream
old newspaper to cover the table
at least four people who agree to look at the blots; eight gives a better count
a notebook and a pencil to write each answer

projects.safety: Use washable paint and cover the table. Keep paint away from mouths and eyes, and wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Make six blots by folding paper over drops of paint. Leave them to dry.
Show every blot to people, one at a time, and write down what each person sees first and what else they see.
Sort the answers into kinds, count them, and set up a gallery with the most surprising answers.

projects.record: A table with a row for each blot and a column for each person. Write the first thing each person saw. Then count how many answers fell into each kind: animal, person, plant, thing, or nothing.
projects.context: In this project, you make six paint blots and ask eight people what they see in each, to find out how differently people read the same shape.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded in half with a few spoonfuls of washable paint dripped on one side and a child pressing the paper flat.
setup.caption: 1. Drop paint on one half of a folded sheet. Fold and press.

setup.art: The sheet opened out to show a symmetrical blot with colours spreading, and six blots drying on a line.
setup.caption: 2. Open it up. Make six blots and let them dry.

setup.art: A child showing a blot to a grandmother who is pointing and describing what she sees, while the child writes in a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Show each blot to eight people and write what they see first.

flow.do: Cover the table with newspaper. Fold a sheet of paper in half and open it. Put three or four drops of paint on one half. Fold the paper again and press it flat with your hand, then open it. Make six blots and lay them out to dry.
flow.say: Fold the paper in half. Put a few drops of paint on one side. Press it shut, and open it. What do you see in the shape? Make six, with different colours.
flow.kid: Fold the paper. Drop paint on one half. Press and open it. Make six.

ask.q: Do you think everyone will see the same thing in the same blot? Why?
good: No, because everyone has seen different things in their life.
Some people will, because the shape is clear.
It depends on how the person is feeling.

flow.parent: Use small drops, and press gently. If the paper gets wet and soggy, use less paint. Leave the blots to dry. The blots are for fun and for finding out how people see. They do not show anything about a person. Paint that is too thick does not spread, and paint that is too watery soaks through, so test one blot first. In damp weather the blots take a day or more to dry. Leave them in a breezy place and begin day 2 only when they are dry. With 2 to 4 children, each child makes three blots and then shows them to the others, but not to the people who will be asked what they see.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Blot Gallery. You make six paint blots.

flow.do: Show each blot to eight people, one at a time. Ask: what is the first thing you see? Write the answer. Then ask: what else could it be? Write that too. Do not say what you see yourself.
flow.say: Look at this shape. What is the first thing you see? What else could it be? Take your time.
flow.kid: Show each blot to eight people. Ask what they see first.
flow.parent: Ask for the first thing, and then what else. Do not suggest answers or react. Some people will see an animal at once, and some will say nothing. If a person is not sure, they may pass. Show the blots to at least four people, such as the family, grandparents or neighbours. Each blot should be shown to the same people in the same order.
flow.wait: Ask all eight people during day 2.
flow.context: This is the second day of the Blot Gallery. You show the blots to people.

flow.do: Sort all the answers into five kinds: animal, person, plant, thing and nothing. Count each kind. Pick the five most surprising answers. Set up the blots with the best answers beside them. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Let us sort all the answers. How many animals? How many people? Which answer surprised you most? Did two people ever see the same thing?
flow.kid: Sort the answers into kinds. Count each kind. Pick the most surprising.

check.q: Two people see different things in the same blot. What is the best explanation?
options: The blot fits many readings, and each brain picks one using its own memories
One of them is wrong and one is right
The blot changed between the two looks
check.why: A blot has no single meaning. The brain looks for a familiar shape, and which shape it finds depends on what that person has seen and expects. Neither person is wrong, and the blot did not change.

flow.context: This is the last day of the Blot Gallery. You sort the answers and set up the gallery.

challenges.title: Hide the Beetle: the best camouflage in plain view
challenges.problem: Make a small paper beetle and hide it in plain view in a room, so that people take the longest time to find it. The beetle must not be covered or hidden behind anything. Anyone with good eyes must be able to see it if they look in the right place.
constraints: The beetle must be no longer than 4 centimetres.
The watcher must be able to see the beetle from where they sit. It must not be covered or hidden behind anything.
You may colour and shape the beetle, and you may choose where to put it, but you may not change the background.
You have five watchers, and each looks for up to 60 seconds.
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts the paper with the scissors. Do not put anything where a person could trip over it.
materials: a room with a patterned cloth, a curtain, a calendar or a mat
general: Colour the beetle the same colour as the background where it sits.
Put the beetle on a pattern that has a similar colour and shape, such as a cloth with many small spots.
Make the beetle a shape that is common in the background, such as a leaf-like shape on a leafy cloth.
creative: Paint stripes across the beetle that carry on the lines of the background, so that the outline of the beetle is broken up.
Put the beetle among a group of other small things of similar size and colour, such as a few black seeds or buttons.
Make the beetle flat and grey and put it on a patch of the wall that has a shadow.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your beetle and your hiding place. Say which trick you are using: matching the background, or breaking the outline. Test with five watchers and write the time each takes. Change one thing and test again with five new watchers.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about camouflage. You use what you know about how the brain groups things and what it expects, to make something hard to find.

setup.art: A child drawing three beetle designs on paper, one plain brown, one with stripes, one spotted, with a patterned cloth beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three beetle designs. Pick the best hiding place.

setup.art: A small paper beetle with stripes sitting on a patterned cloth, almost invisible.
setup.caption: 2. Make the beetle and set it in its place.

setup.art: A watcher looking around a room while a child holds a stopwatch, with a score sheet beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Time each watcher up to 60 seconds. Write the time.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Talk about what makes a thing easy to find: its colour, its outline and its place. Ask your child to draw three beetle designs and pick the best hiding place.
flow.say: A hunter finds a beetle by colour, outline and place. How can you make a beetle hard to find on a cloth or a wall? Draw three ideas.
flow.kid: What makes a beetle hard to find? Draw three ideas.

ask.q: What are two tricks that an animal can use to be hard to find?
good: Look like the background.
Break up her outline with stripes.
Stay among things that look the same.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Hide the Beetle challenge. You plan your beetle and its hiding place.

flow.do: Make the beetle from paper. A grown-up cuts it out. Colour it. Put it in its place in the room, in plain view. Watchers sit at a fixed spot and look for it, up to 60 seconds each. Write the time each takes. Do the test with five watchers.
flow.say: Make your beetle and put it in place. The watchers sit here and look. Press the stopwatch when they start. Stop it when they point to the beetle.
flow.kid: Make the beetle. Put it in place. Time each watcher.
flow.parent: Watchers must not see the hiding place being prepared. Use five new watchers for the second test, because the first five will remember where the beetle was.
flow.context: In this step, you make the beetle, hide it in plain view and time five watchers.

flow.do: Add up the times. Change one thing about the beetle or its place. Test again with five new watchers. Compare the two averages.
flow.say: What was the average time? Change one thing. Then test again with new watchers. Did it get harder to find?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again with five new watchers.
flow.parent: Change only one thing at a time. If the second beetle is found faster, that is a result too, and tells you what does not work.
flow.context: In this step, you improve the beetle by changing one thing and testing again.

challenges.title: Draw a Two-Way Picture: half see a vase, half see faces
challenges.problem: Draw a picture in black lines on white paper that people read in two ways. Ten people look at it. The best picture is the one where the readings split as close to five and five as possible.
constraints: The picture must be drawn in black lines only, with no words and no colour.
The picture must fit inside a square 10 centimetres wide.
The picture must be able to be read as two different things.
You must test the picture with ten people who have not seen it before, and write what each person saw first.
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts any paper with the scissors, if you want to make a frame.
materials: white paper and a black pen
ten people who agree to look
paper and a pencil for tallies
general: Draw a duck that is also a rabbit, with a shape that can be a beak or two ears.
Draw a vase that is also two faces looking at each other.
Draw a cube made of lines that can point two ways.
creative: Draw a banana that is also a boat, with a curve that can be the fruit or the hull.
Draw a cloud that is also a sheep, with a curly outline that can be either.
Draw an eye that is also a leaf, with a pointed shape that suits both.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your picture and name the two readings you meant. Test it with ten people and write what each saw first. Count the split. If it is not close to five and five, change one thing and test with ten new people.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about pictures with two readings. You make something that the brain can read in two ways, and find out how people split.

setup.art: A child's page of five small sketches, each a shape that could be read two ways, with a duck-rabbit and a banana-boat.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some shapes that could be read two ways.

setup.art: The best sketch redrawn large in black pen inside a square 10 centimetres wide.
setup.caption: 2. Redraw the best one in black lines inside a square.

setup.art: A page with a tally of ten marks split between two readings, six for one and four for the other.
setup.caption: 3. Ask ten people what they see first. Tally the readings.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at two-way pictures in a book, or at the cube drawing, the vase and faces drawing and the duck-rabbit drawing. Ask your child to sketch five ideas, each a shape that might be read two ways.
flow.say: What can a curved line be? What can a pointed shape be? Sketch five shapes that could be two different things.
flow.kid: Sketch five shapes that could be two different things.

ask.q: What makes a picture easy to read in only one way?
good: Too many clues for one reading.
A lot of detail that fits only one thing.
A very clear outline.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Draw a Two-Way Picture challenge. You sketch ideas.

flow.do: Redraw the best sketch in black pen inside a 10 centimetre square. Write on the back the two readings you meant. Show it to ten people, one at a time, and ask what they see first. Make a tally of the readings.
flow.say: Draw your best idea neatly in black. Show it to ten people. Ask each one: what is the first thing you see? Keep a tally.
flow.kid: Draw it neatly in black. Ask ten people what they see first.
flow.parent: Do not tell people what to look for. If people suggest a third reading, write it as other.
flow.context: In this step, you draw your picture and test it with ten people.

flow.do: Count the split. Is it close to five and five? Change one thing about the picture and test with ten new people. Compare the two splits.
flow.say: How did the ten people split? Was it close to five and five? Change one thing, and ask ten new people. Is it closer?
flow.kid: Count the split. Change one thing. Test with ten new people.
flow.parent: A picture that splits nine and one has one strong reading. A split near five and five means both readings are about equally good. Change one thing at a time so you know what made the difference.
flow.context: In this step, you count the split and improve the picture.

videos.title: selective attention test
videos.why: To try the counting test yourself, and see how easy it is to miss something large when your attention is elsewhere.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). A parent should preview it first.

videos.title: How the brain turns lines into a cube: ambiguous pictures
videos.why: To see the Necker cube, the vase and faces, and the duck-rabbit explained, with the brain choosing one reading at a time.
videos.check: Not yet found. Find one, watch it, and check that it says the picture does not change and that the brain flips between two readings.

videos.title: Camouflage: Animal Hide & Seek
videos.why: To see leaf insects, nightjars and other animals that disappear against their backgrounds, and how they do it.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). A parent should preview it first.

quiz.p: A drawing that can be read as a vase or as two faces is called what?
opts: An ambiguous picture
A mirror image
A shadow
quiz.why: Ambiguous means able to mean two things equally well. The brain shows one reading at a time and switches between them.

quiz.p: When you see the two faces in the vase and faces drawing, what does the vase become?
opts: The background behind the faces
A bigger vase
Part of the faces
quiz.why: The brain picks one part as the figure in front. The other part becomes the ground behind it. The paper has not changed.

quiz.p: A driver on a phone looks straight at a red light and does not see it. What is the best explanation?
opts: The driver's attention is on the call, so the light is not noticed
The light is too dim for any eye
The driver's eyes were closed
quiz.why: Looking at something does not mean noticing it. Detailed seeing needs attention, and attention was on the call.

quiz.p: A card is held over a tray for a second, and a big thing on the tray changes. Why might a watcher miss it?
opts: There is no movement to catch the eye, and the brain does not compare the two scenes
The change was too small to see
The watcher was not looking at the tray
quiz.why: In plain sight, a change brings movement, which draws attention at once. When something hides the moment, the brain has to compare before and after, and often does not.

quiz.p: Why do many people miss the extra word in 'Paris in the the spring'?
opts: The brain expects the familiar phrase and passes over the repeat
The extra word is written in light ink
The eyes cannot read two words that are the same
quiz.why: The brain reads familiar phrases by guessing what is next. It saw 'the' and expected 'spring', so the repeat was not noticed.

quiz.p: A person looks for a missing key and keeps passing it. What may be happening?
opts: Their search image does not match how the key looks now
The key is invisible
Keys cannot be found by looking
quiz.why: A search image helps you find what you picture, and hides what does not match. If the key looks different from the picture in your mind, you may pass it.

quiz.p: Three circles with a slice missing each are placed so that a triangle appears. Where are the triangle's edges?
opts: The brain makes them, and they are not drawn
Drawn in very thin lines
In the white paper
quiz.why: The brain joins the three circles into one shape and supplies the missing edges. Nerve cells have been found that respond to such edges as if they were real.

quiz.p: A photo of a person is harder to recognise when it is upside down. What does this suggest?
opts: The brain has a special way of reading upright faces
The person's face changes when it is upside down
Photos cannot be turned
quiz.why: Faces are harder to recognise upside down than other objects are. This suggests that the brain reads upright faces all at once, in a special way.

quiz.p: A bee sees dark stripes on a flower that looks plain to you. What is the best explanation?
opts: The stripes are in ultraviolet light, which bees can see and we cannot
The bee is imagining the stripes
The flower changes when a bee comes
quiz.why: Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that guide bees to the nectar. Our eyes cannot sense ultraviolet light, so the flower looks plain to us.

quiz.p: A moth with a pattern that runs across the edge of her wings is found less often by birds. Why?
opts: The pattern breaks up the outline, so the brain does not read the shape as a moth
The moth is smaller
Birds cannot see patterns
quiz.why: Patterns that cut across the edge break up the outline. The hunter's brain joins the pieces to the background instead of to each other.

quiz.p: You want to find out whether trying to hold a cube drawing in one reading changes the number of flips. What must you keep the same?
opts: The drawing, the distance, the light and the time
The person's name
The colour of the pen
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the drawing, the distance or the time changed too, you could not tell what made the difference.

quiz.p: Four people see different things in the same paint blot. What can you say?
opts: The blot fits many readings, and each brain picks one using its own experience
Three of them are wrong
The blot changed four times
quiz.why: A blot has no single meaning. Each brain looks for a familiar shape and finds one that fits what it has seen and expects.

items.p: A cube drawn with lines flips by itself, though the paper does not change. What is the best explanation?
opts: The lines fit two readings, and the brain switches between them
The paper is moving a little
The eyes are tired of the lines
items.why: The same lines could be a cube pointing either way. The brain can show only one reading at a time, so it switches. The paper stays still, and tired eyes are not the main cause.

items.p: A person can see both the vase and the two faces in the vase and faces drawing at the very same moment.
items.why: False. The brain shows one reading at a time. When the faces are the figure, the vase becomes the background, and when the vase is the figure, the faces are the background.

items.p: Missing something large because your attention is on something else is called ____ blindness.
items.why: People who count passes in a video often miss a gorilla that walks across. Their eyes saw the gorilla, but their attention was on the passes.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Figure
the thing the brain picks as being in front
Ground
the background the brain puts behind the figure
Expectation
what the brain thinks is likely before it looks
Camouflage
colours or shapes that make an animal hard to find
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are four words for how the brain reads a scene. The first two describe how it splits a scene into a thing and a background.

items.p: Sort these moments by what the brain is doing.
items: not seeing the doubled 'the' in a familiar phrase
not noticing a gorilla while counting passes
seeing a triangle between three circles with slices missing
seeing a constellation as a hunter
being slow to find a second type of grain after finding the first
not seeing a swapped person while giving directions
items.a: see items
items.why: Expectation helps you read and search quickly, and hides what does not fit. Attention picks a few things to see in detail. Grouping joins separate bits into one whole.

items.p: Many people count only three F's in the sentence FINISHED FILES ARE THE RESULT OF YEARS OF SCIENTIFIC STUDY COMBINED WITH THE EXPERIENCE OF YEARS. There are six. Explain why, using the word 'expect'.
items.a: When we read for meaning, the brain skips small common words such as 'of'. We expect those words, so we do not check them. The F's in 'of' were seen by the eyes, but not noticed.
items.why: A strong answer says that the brain reads by guessing and skips short, familiar words, so some F's are not noticed.

items.p: In the Blink Tray, what made a big change hard to see?
opts: A card hid the moment of change, so there was no movement to catch the eye
The things on the tray were too small
The watchers had their eyes shut
items.why: When the change happens in plain sight, the movement catches the eye at once. When a card hides the moment, the brain has to compare two scenes, and it does that only for a few things at a time.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A cube drawing, a vase and faces drawing, a duck-rabbit drawing, a line measured with a ruler.
items.a: a line measured with a ruler
items.why: The first three can be read in two ways. A line measured with a ruler gives one answer, which is the point of using a ruler.

items.p: Draw three black circles with a slice missing from each. Arrange them so that a triangle appears between them. Draw a dotted line where the brain adds the edge.
items.a: Three circles at the corners of a triangle with the missing slices pointing to the middle, and dotted lines joining the slices where the triangle's edges are seen.
items.why: The brain joins the circles into one shape and makes the edges that are not drawn.

items.p: Label the vase and faces drawing: the vase, a face, and the shared edge.
items.why: The vase and the faces share the same edge. Whichever the brain picks as the figure, the other becomes the background.
items.art: A vase and faces drawing in black and white, with three blank label lines pointing at the white vase, one of the black faces, and the wavy edge between them.

items.p: A photo of a face looks strange when its eyes and mouth are turned upside down, but only when the photo is upright. What does this suggest?
opts: The brain reads an upright face as a whole and notices what is wrong
The brain cannot see upside-down photos
The eyes do not work upside down
items.why: An upright face is read all at once, so a wrong part stands out. An upside-down face is read part by part, and the wrong parts hide. The brain can see upside-down faces, but less well.

items.p: Put these in order: what happens when you read 'Paris in the the spring' aloud and do not notice the extra word.
items: your brain guesses what comes next
you read the phrase aloud as if it were normal
a: your brain guesses what comes next
you read the phrase aloud as if it were normal
items.why: The eyes take in both words. The brain, expecting a familiar phrase, passes over the repeat, so you read it as normal.

items.p: Seeing a face in a plug socket shows that a person's eyes are faulty.
items.why: False. The brain's face finder responds to any rough pattern of two eyes above a mouth. It is a useful habit, because missing a real face matters more than being fooled by a socket.

items.p: Two friends, Lavanya and Imran, talk about a video in which a person in a gorilla suit walks through a ball game while viewers count the passes.

views.says: I would never miss a gorilla. People who miss it are not paying attention.
About half of the people miss it, because they are paying attention to the passes.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you know about attention. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Imran, because missing the gorilla comes from attention being used on the passes, not from carelessness. It can say that Lavanya is right that attention matters, and that if you were told to look for a gorilla, you would not miss the gorilla.
items.why: Missing a large thing is normal when attention is elsewhere. People miss the gorilla because they are paying attention to the passes.

items.p: A tiger's stripes in tall dry grass help her hide. What is the best name for this trick?
opts: Breaking up her outline
Making a loud noise
Looking bigger
items.why: Dark and light stripes cut across the edge of the tiger's body, so the brain does not read the outline as one animal. The stripes do not make her bigger or noisier.

items.p: A mental picture of what you are looking for is called a search ____.
items.why: A search image helps you find the thing you are looking for, and it hides things that do not match.

items.p: Why does the brain show only one reading of an ambiguous picture?
opts: A body must act on one reading at a time
The eyes can only see half of a picture
The paper only has one meaning
items.why: You cannot reach for a cube that is both near and far. The brain picks the likeliest reading so the body can act. The eyes can see the whole picture, and the picture has two readings.

items.p: A bird has eaten green caterpillars for a week. What is she most likely to do next?
opts: Miss a brown caterpillar right next to her beak
Find every kind of caterpillar equally well
Stop looking for food
items.why: A search image for green caterpillars helps the bird find them fast, and makes brown ones easier to miss. Searching for one kind of thing tends to hide others.

items.p: Match each idea to the example that shows it.
pairs: Colour constancy
a white shirt looks white in sunlight and under a lamp
Inverted face effect
a friend's photo is harder to recognise upside down
Change blindness
a big change goes unseen when a flash hides it
Umwelt
a tick's world is the smell of sweat and the warmth of a body
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each idea describes a way in which seeing is built by the brain, or by the body of the animal doing the seeing.

items.p: Sort these by which animal's world they belong to.
items: a strong cloud of smell from a plate of food
the heat of a warm mouse in the dark
fewer colours than a person sees
pits on the face that sense warmth
items.a: see items
items.why: Each kind of animal senses part of the world. A dog's world is rich in smell, a bee's in ultraviolet, and a pit viper's in heat.

items.p: If a photo looks blue and black to one person and white and gold to another, the photo must have two different sets of colours.
items.why: False. The photo has one set of colours. The brain removes the colour of the light it expects, and people who expect different light see different colours.

items.p: Two people look at the same photo of a dress. One sees blue and black, the other sees white and gold. Give the best idea of why, using the word 'light'.
items.a: The photo does not make it clear what light the dress is in. The brain takes away the colour of the light it expects. If one person expects shade and another expects lamp light, they take away different colours and see different dresses.
items.why: A strong answer says that the brain guesses the colour of the light and removes it, and that people may guess differently. It also says that scientists still argue about why people guess differently.

items.p: Draw a tick on a leaf. Show with clouds, arrows or colour what is in the tick's world, and leave the rest of the page blank.
items.a: A tick on a leaf with small clouds of sweat smell and heat lines coming from an animal, and little else.
items.why: A tick's world is mostly the smell of sweat and the warmth of a body. The rest of the world that we see is not part of it.

items.p: Put these in order: how the Thatcher effect shows itself.
items: the changed face looks horrible upright
you turn the changed face upside down
you look at the changed face upright
a: you look at the changed face upright
the changed face looks horrible upright
you turn the changed face upside down
items.why: Upright, the brain reads the face as a whole and notices the wrong parts. Upside down, it reads part by part and the wrong parts do not stand out.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A tiger in tall grass, a nightjar on the ground, a leaf insect on a bush, a bright red poison frog.
items.a: a bright red poison frog
items.why: The tiger, the nightjar and the leaf insect all hide from the brain of a hunter. A bright poison frog stands out on purpose, to warn hunters away.

items.p: Two friends, Revathi and Mohan, talk about seeing faces in clouds and sockets.

views.says: Seeing faces in clouds is a mistake. The brain should not do it.
It is a useful habit. Missing a real face matters more than being fooled by a cloud.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you know about the face finder in the brain. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer may agree with Mohan, because the face finder responds to a rough pattern so as not to miss real faces. It can say that Revathi is right that the face in a cloud is not really there, and that this is a false alarm.
items.why: The same habit finds friends in a crowd and faces in sockets. Scientists treat it as a useful rule that sometimes gives false alarms.

items.p: Ten people look at a drawing. Seven see a vase first and three see faces first. Another drawing splits five and five. Which drawing is the better two-way picture?
opts: The one that splits five and five
The one that splits seven and three
They are the same
items.why: A two-way picture is best when both readings are about equally strong. A five and five split shows that both readings are equally easy to find.

items.p: If the card that hides the moment of change is taken away, watchers see the change at once. What does this show?
opts: The brain notices movement without needing to compare two scenes
The watchers were not paying attention before
The card made the change bigger
items.why: A change that happens in plain sight comes with movement, which draws attention at once. The card removes that movement, so the brain has to compare two scenes.

items.p: Label the ghost triangle drawing: a circle with a slice missing, the edge that is not drawn, and the triangle you see.
a: a circle with a slice missing
the edge that is not drawn
items.why: The brain joins the three circles into one shape and makes edges that are not on the paper.
items.art: Three black circles with wedges removed, arranged around a faint white triangle, with three blank label lines pointing at a circle, a faint triangle edge and the triangle.

items.p: If a person tries hard enough, they can notice everything in a scene.
items.why: False. Attention is limited. Looking hard at one thing means noticing less about others. You can choose what to look for, but you cannot see it all in detail at once.

items.p: A forest guard with sharp eyes looked at a bush for a minute and did not find a leaf insect. Explain why, using the words 'search image'.
items.a: He was looking for a bug sitting on a leaf, and that was his search image. The leaf insect looks like a leaf, so she did not match the search image. His eyes saw her, but his brain did not notice her.
items.why: A strong answer says that the search image helped him find bugs on leaves but made him pass an insect shaped like a leaf.

items.p: Why do stripes across the edge of a body help an animal hide?
opts: They break the outline, so the brain does not read the shape as one animal
They make the animal invisible to the eye
They make the animal look bigger
items.why: The eye still receives the light from the animal. But stripes that run across the edge cut the outline into pieces, which the brain joins to the background instead of to each other.

items.p: Plan a fair test of whether a small change in a scene is noticed more slowly than a big one when a card hides the moment of change. Say what you will change, what you will keep the same, and what you will measure.
items.a: Change which thing changes: a big red cup or a small button. Keep the tray, the card, the timing, the watchers and the number of items the same. Measure how many blinks it takes a watcher to say what changed. Use more than one watcher.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, and counts something. It uses several watchers because one watcher can be lucky.

items.p: Three watchers took 4, 9 and 5 blinks to find a change. What is the best way to report this?
opts: Say all three numbers and the average of 6
Say only the smallest number, 4
Say only the largest number, 9
items.why: Reporting all the numbers and the average shows the whole result and how much it varies. Choosing only the smallest or largest number gives a false picture.

items.p: Two students, Kavitha and Prakash, talk about what seeing is.

views.says: Seeing records the world exactly, like a camera.
Seeing is a best guess that the brain makes, using clues and what it expects.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the cube drawing that flips, the change on the tray that goes unseen, or the F's that people miss. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Prakash, because the cube flipped though the lines did not change, a big change went unseen, and F's were missed because of expectation. It can say that Kavitha is right that the eye does catch light like a camera does, and that most guesses are good.
items.why: The eye does catch light, but the brain builds the seeing from it. Seeing is usually right because the brain's guesses are good, and wrong in the cases we tested.

items.p: When you cover one circle of the ghost triangle, the triangle disappears. What does this show?
opts: The brain needs all three circles to complete the shape
The triangle was drawn in invisible ink
The covered circle was the triangle
items.why: The triangle is made by the brain from the three circles. Remove one circle, and there is nothing to complete. The triangle was never drawn on the paper.

items.p: The brain's choice of what is the thing in front, and what is the background behind it, is called figure and ____.
items.why: In the vase and faces drawing, the vase can be the figure and the faces the ground, or the other way round.

items.p: Sort each result into the idea it supports.
items: the cube drawing flipped though the lines never changed
a gorilla in a video was missed by half the viewers
a bee sees stripes on a flower that looks plain to us
a leaf insect was passed by a sharp-eyed guard
a change was seen only after many blinks
a pit viper senses the heat of a warm mouse
items.a: see items
items.why: Each result shows one idea. The brain guesses and picks one reading. Attention picks a few things to see in detail. And each kind of body senses only part of the world.

items.p: Why must a body pick one reading of what it sees, instead of keeping both? Give one example from an animal.
items.a: A body must act, and it can only do one thing at once. An animal cannot jump towards a branch that is both near and far. So the brain picks the likeliest reading and acts on it. A bird reads a shape in the grass as a worm, and pecks.
items.why: A strong answer says that action needs one reading, and gives an example in which keeping two would not work.

items.p: Draw a shape that can be read as two different things. Label the two readings.
items.a: A shape such as a curved line that can be a banana or a boat, with both readings labelled.
items.why: A shape that fits two readings equally well is read as one at a time, which is what makes a two-way picture.

items.p: In the Blot Gallery, six of eight people saw an animal in one blot. Can you say that all people see animals in blots?
opts: No, because eight people are too few and two saw something else
Yes, because most people saw an animal
Yes, because blots are always animals
items.why: Eight people is a small group, and the answers vary. We can say that animals were the most common answer in our group. We cannot say what all people see.

items.p: If everyone calls a colour red, then everyone must have the same experience of red.
items.why: False. Everyone learns to call that colour red, so they all say red. But nobody can step inside another person to compare what red is like. We can compare what people say and what their nerves do, but not the experience itself.

items.p: Two children, Devi and Arun, talk about the minute they waited.

views.says: A minute is a minute, and it lasts the same time for everybody.
A minute feels different when you wait and when you play, even though the clock is the same.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you know about attention. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer says that both are right in different ways. The clock minute is the same for everyone, as Devi says. The felt minute changes with attention, as Arun says. The word minute is used for two different things.
items.why: A clock measures time. The brain's sense of time is built from attention and an inner clock, and can stretch or shrink.

items.p: Why is it better to ask many watchers than one?
opts: One watcher can be lucky or unlucky, and many show the usual result
Many watchers make the change bigger
One watcher cannot see the tray
items.why: One try can be a fluke. Results from many people show the pattern that most people share, and how much it varies.

items.p: Match each hiding trick to the animal that uses the trick.
pairs: Looking like a leaf, with veins and bite marks
a leaf insect
Looking like a dead leaf when the wings are folded
a leaf butterfly
Stripes that break up the outline in tall grass
a tiger
Looking like a twig, and holding still
a stick insect
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each animal hides by matching what a hunter expects to see, or by breaking up the outline so the brain does not read it as an animal.

items.p: Describe a time when two people read the same thing in two different ways. What clues did each one use?
items.a: For example, two friends read a message that says 'fine' and one thinks the writer is happy while the other thinks the writer is upset. One used the word alone, and one used how the writer usually writes. Both read the same words with different clues.
items.why: A strong answer names a real situation and says what clue each person used, showing that a reading depends on clues and expectation.

items.p: A student wants to know whether upside-down faces are harder to read. Which plan is best?
opts: Show the same faces upright and upside down to several people and score each
Ask one friend which she prefers
Show faces upside down only
items.why: A fair plan changes only the direction of the faces, uses the same faces and gives the same task to several people. To compare, you need both upright and upside-down faces.

applications: Soldiers' uniforms and vehicle paint use patterns of dark and light patches that break up the outline, as a tiger's stripes do.
Road safety teachers explain that a driver on a phone can look at a red light and not see it, because attention is on the call.
Magicians use misdirection. They draw your attention to one hand while the other does the trick.
Airport baggage screeners are trained to look for many kinds of dangerous object, since a search image for one kind makes another easy to miss.
Doctors who read scans use checklists, and a second doctor checks the scan, because even experts miss things they are not looking for.
Proofreaders catch spelling mistakes by reading aloud or backwards, because the brain reading for meaning skips over mistakes.
Designers of signs and logos use figure and ground, for example by hiding an arrow in the space between two letters.
Courts take care with the memories of witnesses, since people can miss large things and read the same scene in different ways.
Teachers of reading ask children to check their first reading of a sentence, since the brain takes the likeliest reading first.
Safety signs are placed where people are already looking, since people do not see warnings that are outside their attention.
People with face blindness, who find it hard to recognise faces, are helped by understanding that face reading is a special skill that can be weaker in some people.

open_questions.q: Why does the brain flip between two readings of a drawing, and what decides when it flips?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists see the activity of the brain change at each flip. Some think that the nerve cells for one reading tire, and others think that the brain keeps testing the other reading. Nobody has a full account.

open_questions.q: How does the brain decide what to attend to, and what to leave out?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that attention is limited and can be steered by what is bright, moving or important to you. They do not know how the brain weighs all of these in a moment.

open_questions.q: Do all people see colours in the same way?
open_questions.why_open: Most people have the same colour sensors, so their signals are likely to be alike. Nobody can compare what the colours feel like from the inside.

open_questions.q: Why do some people find it very hard to recognise faces, though their eyesight is good?
open_questions.why_open: Face blindness runs in some families and can follow an injury. Scientists are still finding out which parts of the face skill are affected.

open_questions.q: How does the brain make one steady scene from eyes that jump several times a second?
open_questions.why_open: Our eyes make small jumps all the time, yet the world does not seem to jump. Scientists have clues but not a full account.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a bee, a bat or a pit viper?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure what each animal senses. Nobody knows how to find out what the experience is like from the inside.

open_questions.q: Can we ever know the world as it is, apart from any one reading of it?
open_questions.why_open: Every reading is made by a body and a brain. We can compare readings, and test them with instruments, but we cannot step outside all readings. People disagree about what follows.

What is the first thing you see in a cloud today? What else could it be?
Can you find a face in something at home, such as a tap, a window or a plate?
What is on your desk that you have not noticed for a long time?
If a bee could tell you what she sees in a flower, what do you think she would say?
When you wait for the bus, does the minute feel longer than when you are playing? Why?
How do you find your friend in a crowd? What do you look for first?
If two people look at the same dress and see different colours, who is right?
What would you hide in this room, and where, so that it is hard to find?

jokes.j: Why did nobody find the leaf insect?

jokes.j: Why did the tiger love the tall grass?

maths.problem: In Count the Flips, four people saw a cube flip 6, 9, 12 and 5 times in a minute. What is the average? Which person is closest to the average?
maths.answer: The average is 8 flips. The person with 9 flips is closest.
maths.explain: 6 plus 9 plus 12 plus 5 is 32. 32 divided by 4 is 8. The person with 9 is 1 away, the person with 6 is 2 away, and the others are further.
maths.context: In the Count the Flips test, you count how often a cube drawing flips for several people.
maths.why_maths: An average shows what is typical for a group and lets you see which person is unusual.

maths.problem: A cube flips 8 times in 60 seconds. On average, how many seconds does each reading last? If each reading lasts longer than that, are there more flips in a minute or fewer?
maths.answer: 7.5 seconds on average. A reading that lasts longer than that means fewer flips in that minute.
maths.explain: 60 divided by 8 is 7.5. If one reading lasts 12 seconds, there is less time left for others, so there are fewer flips overall.
maths.context: In the Count the Flips test, you count flips in a minute.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the time by the number of flips turns a count into how long each reading lasts.

maths.problem: In the Blink Tray, one blink takes 4 seconds: 1 second under the card and 3 seconds in view. A watcher needed 4 blinks to find the big cup and 9 blinks to find the small button. How many seconds is that for each? How many times as long did the button take?
maths.answer: 16 seconds for the cup and 36 seconds for the button. The button took 2.25 times as long.
maths.explain: 4 blinks times 4 seconds is 16 seconds. 9 blinks times 4 seconds is 36 seconds. 36 divided by 16 is 2.25.
maths.context: In the Blink Tray, a card hides the moment of change and you count blinks until the watcher sees it.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying blinks by the time of one blink turns counts into seconds, and dividing compares the two changes.

maths.problem: Five raters scored the changed face when it was upright: 5, 4, 5, 4 and 5. They scored it when it was upside down: 1, 2, 1, 1 and 2. What is the average for each, and how much higher is the upright average?
maths.answer: The upright average is 4.6 and the upside-down average is 1.4. The upright face scored 3.2 higher.
maths.explain: 5 plus 4 plus 5 plus 4 plus 5 is 23, and 23 divided by 5 is 4.6. 1 plus 2 plus 1 plus 1 plus 2 is 7, and 7 divided by 5 is 1.4. 4.6 minus 1.4 is 3.2.
maths.context: In the Upside-Down Faces test, raters score how strange a changed face looks, upright and upside down.
maths.why_maths: Averages with decimals let you compare two sets of scores and see how large the difference is.

maths.problem: A sentence has 6 F's. Four people count them and find 3, 3, 4 and 6. What fraction of the F's did the first person find? What fraction of the people found all six?
maths.answer: 3 out of 6, which is one half. One out of 4 people, which is one quarter.
maths.explain: The first person found 3 of the 6 F's, which is 3 over 6, or 1 over 2. One of the four people found all of them, which is 1 over 4.
maths.context: In Count the F's, you ask people to count the letter F in a sentence.
maths.why_maths: Fractions show how much of the whole was found, which is clearer than saying a number alone.

maths.problem: Ten people look at two two-way pictures. In picture A, 6 see a vase first and 4 see faces. In picture B, 9 see a vase first and 1 sees faces. What percentage saw a vase first in each? Which picture is the better two-way picture, and why?
maths.answer: Picture A: 60 out of 100. Picture B: 90 out of 100. Picture A is better, because its readings are nearer to equal.
maths.explain: 6 out of 10 is 60 out of 100, and 9 out of 10 is 90 out of 100. A good two-way picture splits close to 50 and 50. Picture A is 10 away from 50, and picture B is 40 away.
maths.context: In the Two-Way Picture challenge, you test your picture with ten people and look at how they split.
maths.why_maths: Percentages let you compare splits from groups of the same size, and show how close a picture is to equal.

maths.problem: In Is a Minute a Minute?, a person said stop at 48 seconds while waiting, and at 75 seconds while busy. How many seconds off a true minute was each? What fraction of a minute is each?
maths.answer: 12 seconds too early, which is one fifth of a minute. 15 seconds too late, which is one quarter of a minute.
maths.explain: 60 minus 48 is 12, and 12 out of 60 is 1 out of 5. 75 minus 60 is 15, and 15 out of 60 is 1 out of 4.
maths.context: In Is a Minute a Minute?, you find out how long people feel a minute lasts when waiting and when busy.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting from 60 shows how far off each guess was, and fractions say how large the error was compared with the whole minute.

maths.problem: In the Blot Gallery, eight people looked at six blots, so there were 48 answers. 20 were animals, 12 were people, 6 were plants, 8 were things and 2 were nothing. Check that the kinds add to 48. What fraction of the answers were animals?
maths.answer: 20 plus 12 plus 6 plus 8 plus 2 is 48. Animals were 20 out of 48, which is 5 out of 12.
maths.explain: 20 plus 12 is 32, plus 6 is 38, plus 8 is 46, plus 2 is 48. 20 over 48 simplifies to 5 over 12, by dividing both numbers by 4.
maths.context: In the Blot Gallery, you sort the answers of eight people into kinds and count them.
maths.why_maths: Adding the kinds and checking the total shows you counted every answer. A fraction shows how common one kind was.

maths.problem: In Hide the Beetle, the first beetle took five watchers 10, 15, 22, 28 and 30 seconds to find. The improved beetle took 25, 38, 40, 45 and 47 seconds. Find the average for each, and say about how many times longer the second took.
maths.answer: The first averaged 21 seconds and the second 39 seconds. The second took a little under twice as long.
maths.explain: 10 plus 15 plus 22 plus 28 plus 30 is 105, and 105 divided by 5 is 21. 25 plus 38 plus 40 plus 45 plus 47 is 195, and 195 divided by 5 is 39. 39 is a little less than 42, which is twice 21.
maths.context: In the Hide the Beetle challenge, you time five watchers looking for a paper beetle.
maths.why_maths: An average over several watchers shows how well a beetle is hidden, and estimating the ratio tells you how much better the new design is.
