roots.context: In Count the Flips, a cube drawing flipped while the paper stayed the same. In the Blink Tray, watchers missed a big change on a tray. In Upside-Down Faces, a changed face looked almost normal upside down. In Hide the Beetle, a paper beetle was hard to find in plain view. Now we ask what these tests tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your brain never shows you 'maybe'. When a drawing could mean two things, you see only one of them at a time. The other one disappears, and you cannot see both at once.
deep_truth.habit: We talk as if seeing were like a camera, which could record a scene that has two readings and keep both. But a body has to act on one reading at a time, so the brain must pick, and it does not tell you that it picked.
deep_truth.evidence: In Count the Flips, the lines on the paper never changed, yet the cube flipped several times a minute, and you saw only one version each time. Trying to hold one version slowed the flips for many people, but usually did not stop them.

three.who_am_i: Each of us sees the world in one way. That way is a reading, which our brain has chosen from many that could fit the same light and sound. The reading depends on what we expect, what we attend to and the body we have.
three.what_is_life: Every living being has to pick one reading and act. A tick waits for the smell of sweat, a bee heads for patterns in ultraviolet, and a chick looks for the grain she expects. Each lives in the reading their body can make.
three.what_is_this_world: The world gives the same light to every eye. What anyone sees depends on that light and also on their own body and brain. Nobody sees the world without a body and a brain doing the seeing.

roots.thread: Light, sound and smell come from the same world to every creature. A body turns them into one reading so that it can act: reach, run, hide or hunt. Because a particular body makes the reading, the same cube can flip, the same tray can change unseen, and the same flower can be a bright target for a bee and a plain one for you. The world is not made up by the brain. But the way it appears to anyone always depends on both the world and a body that has to choose one reading.

teachings.teaching: Zhuang Zhou dreamed that he was a butterfly, happily flying about. He did not know that he was Zhou. When he woke, he was Zhou again. He did not know whether he was Zhou who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming that he was Zhou.
teachings.link: Two readings of one life both fit, as the two cubes fit one drawing. Zhuangzi leaves the question open and does not pick a reading, which is a hard thing for a brain to do.

teachings.teaching: The hymn asks where everything came from, and ends by saying that the one who watches over it from the highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps even he does not know.
teachings.link: The hymn ends with a maybe, which the brain never shows us in what we see. It lets a question stay open instead of closing it with one reading.

teachings.teaching: Prisoners in a cave, who have only ever seen shadows on a wall, take the shadows for the real things. One prisoner is freed and sees the brighter world outside. He comes back to tell the others, and they do not believe him.
teachings.link: A reading can feel like the whole truth because it is the only one we have. Tests, such as the tray and the cube, are ways to step out of one reading and see how it was made.

science.text: A picture that fits two readings is seen as one reading at a time, and the brain switches between them without the viewer choosing. This has been known since Necker, in 1832.

The brain may settle on a reading by combining what its senses report with what it expects, in the way a scientist weighs an idea against the evidence. This is a main idea in brain science today, called predictive processing.
Why the brain flips, and what a reading feels like from the inside, are not known.

other_view.view: The two readings are two states of a network of nerve cells that compete and then tire. Words such as 'choice' or 'reading' only describe the competition. The science needs only the nerve cells and their activity.

practice.title: Hold two readings
practice.say: Look at the cube drawing. Notice the reading you see now. Breathe slowly. Wait until it flips. When it does, whisper the word 'now'. Then try to see both readings at once, and notice that you cannot. Quietly say the word 'maybe'.
practice.kid: Look at the cube. Breathe slowly. When it flips, whisper 'now'. Try to see both readings. Say 'maybe'.

ask: When you see a face in a cloud, who is making the face: the cloud or you?
What is the first thing you see in a new person or a new place? What other reading might you be missing?
If a bee sees a flower differently, which of you sees the true flower?

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people thought the eye worked like a camera, so that anything drawn the same way would always look the same. In 1832, a Swiss crystal expert named Louis Albert Necker was studying drawings of crystals. He noticed something odd. A drawing of a simple crystal sometimes seemed to turn inside out by itself, with the front corner suddenly becoming the back. He wrote to a science magazine to say that the drawing had not changed and he had not moved. Only what he saw had changed. Later in the same century, the German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz suggested that the brain draws conclusions from the light it receives, without our noticing. He called this unconscious inference. Over the next 150 years, tests showed this again and again, from drawings that flip, to people who miss a gorilla walking across a screen. The cube drawing is still called the Necker cube.
how_we_found_out.who: Louis Albert Necker, a Swiss crystal expert (1786 to 1861), and Hermann von Helmholtz, a German scientist (1821 to 1894)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The idea that the eye works like a camera, so that a drawing always looks the same. Necker showed that one unchanging drawing can look different from moment to moment.
